what_would_settle_it: An incident-use, active-comparator cohort comparing people who start a benzodiazepine with people who start another treatment for the same anxiety or sleep problem, with exposure assessed 10 or more years before a research-standard dementia diagnosis, education, socioeconomic status, alcohol and the course of anxiety and sleep problems measured, and absolute risks reported.

domains.note: No data on education, socioeconomic status, smoking or alcohol (p. 4); the reasons for prescribing are known only from claims diagnoses absent for most people who filled prescriptions; anxiety and sleep problems that precede Alzheimer's disease may begin more than 5 years before diagnosis, which the authors acknowledge as an alternative explanation (p. 4).

Dispensing claims avoid recall bias but not non-adherence; the window lasts 1 to 5 years depending on follow-up; the reference group includes anyone who started benzodiazepines only in the last 5 years; z-drugs not considered.

Incidence density sampling within one insured population is appropriate, but cases are a narrow subset (4.6% of sampled dementia claimants) after combined exclusions for other dementias or earlier anti-dementia treatment, and controls come from a separate random sample.
Not relevant to the contrast; continued use after the window is described (64.8% vs 60.6% still treated at the index date).
Complete claims for enrolled members; no exclusions for missing covariates are reported.

Physician claims diagnosis without validation against research criteria and with possible recording delay; people taking benzodiazepines may be seen more often, or show drug-related cognitive symptoms that prompt assessment (the authors' analysis by treatment status at diagnosis argues against the latter).
No protocol; several exposure classifications and two models; the abstract reports model 1, in which the 91–180 category is significant, whereas in model 2 it is not.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A large, well-matched claims study with a deliberate 5-year lag and a gradient by cumulative amount, but confounding by the reasons for prescribing, prodromal symptoms and unmeasured education and socioeconomic status is not controlled, so the association cannot be read as an effect of the drugs. Cite for: the association and its gradient in Quebec claims data (no association up to about 3 months' supply; odds ratio about 1.8 above 6 months). Do not cite for: a causal increase in risk, absolute risks or numbers of excess cases.

key_findings.finding: Cases came from a random sample of 38,741 Quebec drug-plan members aged over 66 with dementia-related claims (controls from a separate sample of 86,259 without): people with a first claims diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (ICD-9 331.0) in 2000–2009, no earlier other dementia or anti-dementia treatment, and at least 6 years of prior follow-up. 1,796 qualified after 31,769 were excluded for non-Alzheimer dementia or earlier anti-dementia treatment and 5,176 for under 6 years' follow-up; each was matched to 4 controls (7,184) on sex, age group and follow-up length.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study design and setting; Selection of cases and controls (p. 2); Results › Study population (p. 3); Figure (p. 10)
key_findings.note: The exclusion counts (31,769 and 5,176) are printed only in the flow chart on p. 10, an image without a text layer, and were checked on the rendered page; 86,259 is broken across two lines on p. 2 and was also checked on the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: Ever use: 894 of 1,796 cases (49.8%) and 2,873 of 7,184 controls (40.0%) had filled at least one benzodiazepine prescription 5 to 10 years before the index date; adjusted odds ratio 1.51 (95% CI 1.36 to 1.69), and 1.43 (1.28 to 1.60) after also adjusting for anxiety, depression and insomnia diagnoses.
key_findings.locator: Results › Main analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 3); Table 3 (p. 9)

key_findings.finding: The association depended on cumulative amount: up to 90 prescribed daily doses (about 3 months), 13.0% of cases vs 14.6% of controls, odds ratio 1.09 (0.92 to 1.28), no association; 91–180 doses, 3.9% vs 3.6%, 1.32 (1.01 to 1.74), falling to 1.28 (0.97 to 1.69) with anxiety, depression and insomnia added; above 180 doses (over 6 months), 32.9% vs 21.8%, 1.84 (1.62 to 2.08), and 1.74 (1.53 to 1.98) in the fuller model.
key_findings.locator: Results › Main analysis, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); Table 3 (p. 9)

key_findings.finding: By half-life: short-acting drugs (under 20 hours) were filled by 32.6% of cases vs 27.8% of controls, odds ratio 1.43 (1.27 to 1.61); long-acting drugs (20 hours or more) by 17.2% vs 12.2%, 1.70 (1.46 to 1.98).
key_findings.locator: Results › Main analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 3); Table 3 (p. 9)

key_findings.finding: Moving the index date back one year (exposure counted 6 to 10 years before diagnosis) left the results unchanged: ever use 1.50 (1.35 to 1.68); up to 3 months 1.11 (0.94 to 1.30); 3 to 6 months 1.56 (1.21 to 2.01); over 6 months 1.79 (1.58 to 2.04).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Exposure assessment, last paragraph (p. 2); Results › Sensitivity analysis (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Among people with more than 6 months' use, the odds ratio was 1.72 (1.51 to 1.97) when treatment was still under way at diagnosis and 2.51 (1.97 to 3.20) when it had stopped at least a year earlier. These subgroup estimates are given only in the Discussion, without counts, a table or the model used, and the authors cite them to argue that confounding of the diagnosis by the drugs' effects on cognition seems unlikely. Treatment was still active at the index date in 64.8% of cases and 60.6% of controls (as printed; read here as shares of people with any use, since 64.8% of all 1,796 cases would be 1,164, more than the 894 with any use).
key_findings.locator: Results › Main analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Discussion › Strengths and limitations, 2nd paragraph on p. 4

key_findings.finding: Claims diagnoses of the main reasons for prescribing were recorded for far fewer people than filled prescriptions (editors' reading): anxiety in 21.4% of cases vs 15.1% of controls, depressive symptoms in 2.9% vs 2.4% and insomnia in 4.0% vs 3.2%, against benzodiazepine fills in 49.8% vs 40.0%. The authors acknowledge that these symptoms could have been under-reported when they were not the physician's main diagnosis, but say the anxiety and depression figures do not seem to depart markedly from prevalences reported for people over 65. No significant interaction was found with any of the three (P = 0.48, 0.75 and 0.99).
key_findings.locator: Results › Main analysis, 3rd paragraph (p. 3); Discussion › Strengths and limitations, 4th paragraph on p. 4; Table 2 (p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Other recorded differences: myocardial infarction was less common in cases (3.4% vs 4.6%), and stroke (7.0% vs 5.8%), hypercholesterolaemia (20.9% vs 16.5%) and anxiety more common. The database holds no information on socioeconomic status, education, smoking or alcohol; the authors note that the missing adjustment for socioeconomic and educational level could bias the results, and argue that not adjusting for smoking and alcohol was likely conservative, as benzodiazepine use is thought to be higher in regular drinkers and chronic wine drinking has been claimed to be protective.
key_findings.locator: Results › Main analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Table 2 (p. 8); Discussion › Strengths and limitations, 5th paragraph on p. 4

key_findings.finding: Alzheimer's disease was taken from physician diagnoses in claims data. As evidence against misclassification the authors cite the drug plan's rules for reimbursing cholinesterase inhibitors (a Mini-Mental State score of 10 to 26 to start, evidence of benefit to continue), met by 72% of cases. They also argue that misclassification between cases and controls would make the estimates more conservative, which holds when the misclassification is unrelated to benzodiazepine use (editors' note).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths and limitations, 5th and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors acknowledge that anxiety and sleep disorders, two main reasons for prescribing, may go with early amyloid changes and that benzodiazepine use might therefore be an early marker of a condition that raises dementia risk rather than its cause.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths and limitations, last paragraph

key_findings.finding: In their implications the authors write that a 43–51% increase in risk among people who use benzodiazepines would generate a huge number of excess cases and that use beyond 3 months should be weighed carefully; no absolute risk or excess-case number is calculated.
key_findings.locator: Implications for clinical practice and public health, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says that adding anxiety, depression and insomnia altered neither the strength nor the significance of the association (p. 3), and the abstract gives 1.32 (1.01 to 1.74) for 91–180 prescribed daily doses; but in Table 3 that category loses significance in the fuller model (1.28, 0.97 to 1.69).
reporting_issues.consequence: The middle step of the dose gradient is not robust to that adjustment; only the over-6-months category stays clearly raised. Gray et al. (2016, p. 6) make the same observation.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 classifies benzodiazepines at a 20-hour half-life cut-off, yet chlordiazepoxide (listed 5–30 h) and nitrazepam (16–48 h) are classed as long-acting and alprazolam and lorazepam (10–20 h) as short-acting; the rule for drugs whose listed range spans 20 hours is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison of long- with short-acting drugs depends on classifications the paper does not explain.

reporting_issues.issue: The flow chart counts the exclusions for non-Alzheimer dementia and for anti-dementia treatment before diagnosis together (31,769), so it is unknown how many were excluded for each reason.
reporting_issues.consequence: It cannot be judged whether the large exclusion of earlier-treated or mixed cases selected cases in a way related to benzodiazepine use.

reporting_issues.issue: The citation line reads BMJ 2104;349:g5205, while the page headers give 2014.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical only; the reference record (2014) is correct.

design_detail: Prospective population-based cohort (Adult Changes in Thought, ACT, within the Group Health integrated health system, Seattle): 3,434 adults aged 65 or over without dementia at entry and with at least 10 years of prior Group Health membership, screened every 2 years with the Cognitive Abilities Screening Instrument (CASI) and evaluated for dementia with research criteria; mean follow-up 7.3 years. Exposure: total standardized daily doses (TSDDs) of benzodiazepines (and the few non-benzodiazepine hypnotics) dispensed in a rolling 10-year window that excluded the most recent year, from pharmacy records, as a time-varying exposure in Cox models with age as the time scale. Cognitive trajectory analysed in 3,993 participants with generalized estimating equations.
can_establish: Whether, in this insured older US population followed with research-standard dementia diagnosis, people with more cumulative benzodiazepine dispensing over the previous 10 years developed dementia or Alzheimer's disease at higher rates, or declined faster on CASI, than people with none.
cannot_establish: The effect of heavier or longer use than observed here (median of the top category about a year of daily use, and few people with heavy use); effects among people who stopped early or developed dementia before enrolment (the cohort followed people already taking or not taking benzodiazepines); causation in either direction; or results for non-white or less-educated populations.

sample.recruitment: Random sample of Group Health members aged 65 or over without dementia in the Seattle area: 2,581 enrolled in 1994–96, 811 in 2000–03, then continuous enrolment from 2004 to replace people who developed dementia, died or dropped out (p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Of 4,724 ACT participants, 676 were excluded (2 withdrew consent for use of Group Health data; 674 had under 10 years of membership before baseline). The dementia analyses required at least one follow-up visit (614 excluded), leaving 3,434; the trajectory analyses required a valid baseline CASI (55 excluded), leaving 3,993, and dropped visits after dementia onset (Fig 1, p. 2).
sample.demographics: Median age at entry 74.4 (IQR 70–80); 60% women; 91% white (3,134); 66% some college education (Table 2; p. 4). Heavier-use groups had more women, more fair or poor self-rated health, more high depressive symptoms and more comorbidity (Table 2, p. 4).
sample.attrition: 25,019 person-years, mean 7.3 (SD 4.8) years, until dementia onset, disenrolment or the last visit before 30 September 2012 (pp. 3–4). 130 observations (3.8%) with missing covariates were excluded from the adjusted models (p. 4; Table 5 footnote). The 614 people without a follow-up visit (15% of the 4,048 eligible; editors' calculation) are not described.
sample.selection_effects: Insured, mostly white and relatively well-educated urban population (authors' limitation, p. 8). People were followed whatever their prior benzodiazepine history, so those who developed dementia before 65 or before enrolment were ineligible, and those who stopped after early cognitive side effects stay in the lower categories; the authors say the first could have biased the findings towards no association and call the second a limitation other studies share (p. 8).

exposure.measurement: Group Health computerized pharmacy data (drug, strength, route, date and amount dispensed) (p. 2). Each fill was converted to standardized daily doses by dividing the amount dispensed by the minimum effective daily dose for older adults from a geriatric dosage handbook (Table 1, p. 3), and summed over a rolling 10-year window that excluded the most recent year (Fig 2, p. 3). The paper does not discuss fills outside Group Health pharmacies.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Categories: none, 1–30, 31–120, 121 or more TSDDs, chosen from the distribution of exposure and clinically meaningful cut-points (p. 3); in the top category the median was 375 TSDDs, which the authors equate with slightly over a year of daily use (p. 4). Temazepam, diazepam, clonazepam, triazolam and lorazepam made up 83% of exposure (Table 3, p. 5). For the trajectory analyses the window had no lag, and recent use meant two or more fills in the 6 months before a visit (p. 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Zolpidem, zaleplon and eszopiclone were counted with benzodiazepines; few participants used them (p. 2; Table 3). Current smoking was adjusted for; alcohol and other psychotropic medicines are not mentioned as covariates.

comparison.controls: Person-time with no benzodiazepine dispensing in the lagged 10-year window (time-varying): 16,849 person-years and 511 dementia cases (Table 4, p. 5).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Anxiety and insomnia were not measured as covariates (p. 8); covariates were collected at study entry, so in some cases after exposure had begun, and some may be consequences of use (p. 8).

outcomes.instruments: CASI (0–100) every 2 years; a score of 85 or below triggered a standardized evaluation (physical and neurological examination and neuropsychological testing) and a multidisciplinary consensus diagnosis by DSM-IV and NINCDS-ADRDA criteria, confirmed at a later examination, with onset dated midway between the triggering visit and the previous one (p. 2). Trajectory: CASI and CASI rescaled by item response theory (CASI-IRT) (p. 2).
outcomes.validity_norms: Research-standard diagnosis. The authors note CASI is a screening tool, relatively insensitive to decline in people with high cognitive function, and used IRT rescaling to address this (pp. 2, 8).
outcomes.operationalization: Incident all-cause dementia and possible or probable Alzheimer's disease; mean CASI and its annual rate of change in people not yet diagnosed.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Three exposure levels for two diagnostic outcomes and two cognitive outcomes, plus several sensitivity analyses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not stated whether the consensus panel knew participants' medication use; the screening rule applied to everyone regardless of exposure.

analysis.effect_sizes: Cox hazard ratios against no use (Fig 3, p. 6). Dementia, multivariable, 1-year lag: 1–30 TSDDs 1.25 (1.03 to 1.51); 31–120 1.31 (1.00 to 1.71); 121 or more 1.07 (0.83 to 1.39). Alzheimer's disease: 1.27 (1.03 to 1.57); 1.16 (0.84 to 1.60); 0.95 (0.71 to 1.27). Top category split: 121–364 TSDDs 1.11 (0.78 to 1.58); 365 or more 1.03 (0.73 to 1.44) (p. 5). Two-year lag, lowest category: dementia 1.18 (0.97 to 1.44), Alzheimer's 1.18 (0.95 to 1.47). Post hoc five-year lag (Table 5): dementia 1.21 (0.98 to 1.50), 1.20 (0.88 to 1.64), 1.13 (0.85 to 1.52); Alzheimer's 1.24 (0.98 to 1.57), 1.04 (0.72 to 1.51), 1.05 (0.75 to 1.46). Splines: 1.1 to 1.4 up to about 90 TSDDs, near 1.0 above (Fig 4). Cognition: no group differed significantly from no use in mean CASI or annual change; top group 0.002 points a year slower decline (−0.05 to 0.06) (Table 7). Editors' calculation from Table 4: crude dementia incidence 30.3, 36.1, 39.6 and 30.2 per 1,000 person-years for none, 1–30, 31–120 and 121 or more TSDDs; Alzheimer's 24.8, 29.3, 27.0 and 22.6 (not age-adjusted).
analysis.covariates: Study cohort, age at entry (with age as the time scale), sex, education, BMI, current smoking, regular exercise, self-rated health, treated hypertension, treated diabetes, stroke and coronary heart disease (the last two time-varying) and depressive symptoms (short CES-D of 10 or more) (pp. 3–4). Sensitivity analyses: depressive symptoms as time-varying; Charlson comorbidity index (p. 4).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned. Exposure categories were set from the distribution of exposure and clinically meaningful cut-points and checked with splines (pp. 3–4); the five-year-lag analysis is labelled post hoc (p. 4). Ethics approval from the Group Health and University of Washington institutional review boards; written informed consent (p. 9).
analysis.selective_reporting: Primary, sensitivity and post hoc analyses are all reported, including those that weaken the low-use association.
analysis.power: Not reported. The top exposure category contributed 2,481 person-years and 75 dementia cases (Table 4).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 3,434 older adults followed for a mean of 7.3 years with research-standard diagnosis, dementia was modestly more frequent with low (1–30 TSDDs; hazard ratio 1.25) and moderate (31–120; 1.31) cumulative benzodiazepine use but not with the highest use (121 or more; 1.07, 0.83 to 1.39), whose crude dementia rate (30.2 per 1,000 person-years) equalled that of no use (30.3; editors' calculation). The low-use association weakened with a 2-year lag and disappeared with a 5-year lag; Alzheimer's disease followed the same pattern; cognitive decline did not differ.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that risk is slightly higher with minimal exposure but not with the highest level, and that the results do not support a causal association (p. 1), which matches the data at the exposure levels observed; the discussion limits the conclusion to those levels and concedes that a moderate association in the top group cannot be excluded (pp. 7–8). The abstract does not say that the top category was small (267 people at entry, 75 dementia cases), that its median exposure was about a year of daily use, or that the cohort followed people already taking benzodiazepines, so that susceptible people may have stopped early or developed dementia before enrolment, which would hide a harmful effect (p. 8). A headline that benzodiazepines do not cause dementia would overstate the paper: its interval for the heaviest use reaches a hazard ratio of 1.39, and heavier or longer use than seen here was not studied.

timeline.event: Billioti de Gage et al., prospective population-based study of 1,063 older adults in France (BMJ 2012;345:e6231): new use associated with dementia, hazard ratio 1.62 (1.08 to 2.43); as described here, it relied on periodic interviews without dose or duration and excluded 72% of the sample for its new-use design (p. 6).

Billioti de Gage et al., Quebec claims case-control study: odds ratio 1.84 above 180 prescribed daily doses, no association below 91; this study's interval for its top category excludes an association of that size.

Imfeld et al. (Drug Saf), UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink case-control study: high use not associated with Alzheimer's disease once use started in the prodromal phase was accounted for, as described here (pp. 5–6).

replication.where_it_stands: Contested. Studies relying on claims diagnoses and shorter lags (Billioti de Gage et al., 2014) report associations rising with cumulative use; this cohort, with research diagnoses and data collected from participants, finds a small excess only at low use, consistent with prescribing for early symptoms, and none at the highest use. A meta-analysis on the project's benzodiazepine list that adjusts for protopathic bias (Penninkilampi and Eslick, 2018) was not read for this card.

funding.funder: National Institute on Aging (NIH grants U01AG00678 to EBL and R03AG042930 to SD) and the Branta Foundation (SD); the sponsors had no role in design, conduct, data collection, analysis, interpretation, manuscript preparation or the decision to submit (p. 8).
funding.declared_conflicts: SD received a Merck/American Geriatrics Society New Investigator Award; EB receives royalties from UpToDate; RW received funding as a biostatistician from a research grant awarded to Group Health Research Institute from Pfizer; OY received funding as a biostatistician from research grants awarded to Group Health Research Institute from Amgen and Bayer (p. 9).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of Washington, Group Health Research Institute and the University of Pennsylvania. The competing-interest statement names EB, presumably Eric B Larson (EBL elsewhere in the paper).

what_would_settle_it: An incident-use, active-comparator cohort or target-trial emulation, comparing people who start a benzodiazepine with people who start another treatment for the same anxiety or sleep problem, with research-standard dementia diagnosis, lags of 5 years or more, measured anxiety and sleep problems, and enough people with several years of continuous use to estimate the risk at heavy cumulative exposure.

domains.note: Adjusted for education, smoking, BMI, exercise, self-rated health, cardiovascular conditions and depressive symptoms collected from participants; age-adjusted and fully adjusted estimates are similar. Anxiety and insomnia not adjusted for, and covariates were measured at entry, in some cases after exposure had begun (p. 8).

Ten years of dispensing records (guaranteed by the membership rule) and a standardized dose metric, but dispensing is not consumption, fills outside Group Health are not discussed, and the top category mixes intermittent and sustained use.

People with any prior history of use rather than people starting treatment: those who developed dementia before 65 or before enrolment were ineligible, which the authors say could bias towards no association; the 10-year membership rule and the requirement of a follow-up visit also select.
Prescribers may have stopped benzodiazepines after cognitive changes, which the authors could not ascertain (p. 8); this would move susceptible people into lower categories.
614 of 4,048 eligible participants (15%) excluded for lacking a follow-up visit without description; 130 observations (3.8%) with missing covariates excluded from adjusted models.
Everyone screened every 2 years, with standardized evaluation and consensus research diagnosis; whether the panel knew medication use is not stated, but the screening rule did not depend on exposure.
No registration; exposure cut-points chosen partly from the data, though checked with splines; sensitivity and post hoc analyses are reported openly.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A well-conducted cohort with research-standard diagnosis, prospective covariates and long pharmacy histories, but with few people with heavy, long-term use and a design that can let susceptible people drop out of the higher categories before follow-up, both of which limit how far a null result at the highest use can be generalized. Cite for: no detectable increase in dementia or Alzheimer's disease with the highest cumulative use observed (median about a year of daily use) and a small, lag-sensitive excess at low use. Do not cite as proof that heavy or long-term benzodiazepine use carries no risk.

key_findings.finding: The Adult Changes in Thought study randomly sampled Group Health members aged 65 or over without dementia in the Seattle area (2,581 enrolled 1994–96, 811 in 2000–03, continuous enrolment from 2004). Of 4,724 participants, 676 were excluded (674 with under 10 years of prior membership, 2 withdrew consent for data use) and 614 had no follow-up visit, leaving 3,434 for the dementia analyses; 3,993 with a valid baseline CASI entered the cognitive-trajectory analyses.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Design, study setting, and participants; Fig 1

key_findings.finding: At entry the median age was 74, 60% were women, 91% white and 66% had some college education. 30% had filled at least one benzodiazepine prescription in the previous 10 years, but only 3% (98 people) in the previous 6 months. By cumulative use before entry, 2,416 had none, 492 had 1–30 TSDDs, 259 had 31–120 and 267 had 121 or more.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Heavier use went with poorer health at entry: in the top category compared with no use, fair or poor self-rated health 20.6% vs 13.8%, high depressive symptoms 20% vs 8.6% and coronary heart disease 24% vs 17.4%, with fewer men (32.6% vs 43.5%); college education was similar (65.9% vs 65.8%).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Exposure was the number of standardized daily doses dispensed, summed over a rolling 10-year window that left out the most recent year to avoid counting prescriptions for early symptoms. In the top category (121 or more) the median was 375 TSDDs, which the authors equate with slightly over a year of daily use. Five drugs (temazepam, diazepam, clonazepam, triazolam and lorazepam) made up 83% of exposure.
key_findings.locator: Use of benzodiazepines (pp. 2–3); Fig 2 (p. 3); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 4); Table 3 (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Over 25,019 person-years (mean 7.3, SD 4.8 years), 797 participants (23.2%) developed dementia, 637 of them (79.9%) Alzheimer's disease.
key_findings.locator: Results › Dementia and Alzheimer's disease, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Dementia cases and person-years by cumulative use: none 511 in 16,849; 1–30 TSDDs 148 in 4,099; 31–120 TSDDs 63 in 1,590; 121 or more 75 in 2,481. Editors' calculation: crude incidence of 30.3, 36.1, 39.6 and 30.2 per 1,000 person-years (Alzheimer's disease 24.8, 29.3, 27.0 and 22.6), not adjusted for age.
key_findings.locator: Table 4

key_findings.finding: Adjusted hazard ratios for dementia against no use (1-year lag): 1.25 (95% CI 1.03 to 1.51) for 1–30 TSDDs, 1.31 (1.00 to 1.71) for 31–120 and 1.07 (0.83 to 1.39) for 121 or more; for Alzheimer's disease 1.27 (1.03 to 1.57), 1.16 (0.84 to 1.60) and 0.95 (0.71 to 1.27). Splitting the top category gave 1.11 (0.78 to 1.58) for 121–364 TSDDs and 1.03 (0.73 to 1.44) for 365 or more.
key_findings.locator: Results › Dementia and Alzheimer's disease, 1st paragraph (begins on p. 4; hazard ratios on p. 5); Fig 3 (p. 6)
key_findings.note: The interval for the top dementia category is printed three ways: 0.83 to 1.39 in Fig 3 (primary model), 0.83 to 1.37 in the Results text and 0.82 to 1.39 in the abstract (reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Age-adjusted estimates were similar (dementia 1.33, 1.44 and 1.15). With a 2-year lag the low-use association was no longer significant (dementia 1.18, 0.97 to 1.44; Alzheimer's disease 1.18, 0.95 to 1.47); adding time-varying depressive symptoms or comorbidity changed little; and a post hoc 5-year lag showed no association at any level (dementia 1.21, 1.20 and 1.13 (0.85 to 1.52); Alzheimer's disease 1.24, 1.04 and 1.05 (0.75 to 1.46)).
key_findings.locator: Results › Dementia and Alzheimer's disease, 3rd paragraph (p. 5); Fig 3 and Table 5 (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Modelled continuously with splines, the hazard ratio for dementia was 1.1 to 1.4 up to about 90 TSDDs and fell towards 1.0 at higher exposure.
key_findings.locator: Results › Dementia and Alzheimer's disease, 2nd paragraph; Fig 4 (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Cognitive decline: the baseline CASI averaged 93.4 (SD 4.7) and was similar across exposure groups (93.0 to 93.6). No group differed significantly from no use in mean CASI or in its annual rate of change; the top group declined 0.002 points a year more slowly (−0.05 to 0.06), and people with recent use (two or more fills, each of at least 7 TSDDs, in the 6 months before a visit) did not differ significantly in rate of decline from those without (−0.0061, −0.08 to 0.07). Results were similar with IRT-rescaled scores.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Use of benzodiazepines, last paragraph (p. 3); Results › Cognitive trajectory (p. 5); Tables 6 and 7 (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: The authors write that their confidence limits exclude an association of the size reported by the Quebec case-control study (odds ratio 1.84 above 180 prescribed daily doses) but cannot rule out a moderate association in their top category, and that the Quebec study's claims-based diagnosis, possibly delayed and differentially misclassified, is the main difference between the studies.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Comparison with other studies, 2nd paragraph (p. 6) and its continuation (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Limitations the authors state: few participants had heavy use, and exposure may have been lower than in some other studies; depletion of susceptible people cannot be ruled out, since the no-use group may include people with past use who had acute cognitive adverse effects from the drugs because of preclinical dementia and so did not accumulate more use (a bias they say other studies share), and the most susceptible may have developed dementia at a younger age and been ineligible, which could have biased the findings towards no association; anxiety and insomnia were not adjusted for; in some cases covariates were measured after exposure began; and the sample was mostly white and relatively well educated.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths and limitations, 1st paragraph (begins on p. 7) to 3rd paragraph (p. 8)

reporting_issues.issue: The hazard ratio of 1.07 for dementia in the top exposure category carries three different intervals: 0.82 to 1.39 in the abstract, 0.83 to 1.37 in the Results text, and 0.83 to 1.39 in Fig 3 for the primary 1-year-lag model; the abstract's interval matches the 2-year-lag row of Fig 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Numerically negligible; cite the Fig 3 primary model (0.83 to 1.39).

reporting_issues.issue: In the paragraph on the spline models the text says benzodiazepine use was not significantly associated with Alzheimer's disease at any exposure level, while the categorical analysis in the same section reports a significant hazard ratio for Alzheimer's disease at 1–30 TSDDs (1.27, 1.03 to 1.57).
reporting_issues.consequence: The sentence refers to the spline model only; it should not be cited as a categorical result.

reporting_issues.issue: 614 otherwise eligible participants without a follow-up visit were excluded from the dementia analyses (Fig 1), and their characteristics and benzodiazepine use are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: It cannot be judged whether this exclusion of about 15% of the eligible cohort was related to exposure.

design_detail: Clinical review for prescribers (Australian Prescriber, four pages) by two staff specialists in clinical pharmacology and addiction medicine at Royal Prince Alfred and Concord Repatriation General hospitals, Sydney. It covers prevention, recognition and assessment of benzodiazepine (and z-drug) misuse and dependence, and two management approaches: withdrawal aiming at abstinence, and maintenance as harm reduction. No methods, search or selection criteria; 24 references, including a Cochrane review of pharmacological interventions (Denis et al., 2006), a meta-analysis (Parr et al., 2009) and a Cochrane review (Darker et al., 2015) of psychological interventions, cohort and trial reports, and government sources; a box of withdrawal features and a half-life and equivalence table, both without sources.
can_establish: What two Australian addiction-medicine specialists told prescribers in 2015 about benzodiazepine dependence and withdrawal, and which of their statements rest on cited evidence.
cannot_establish: How often seizures or other severe reactions follow abrupt stopping (no frequencies are given, and the key seizure statements carry no citation), or how management approaches compare beyond what the cited reviews found.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (clinical review). Sources chosen by the authors; no search described.
sample.selection_effects: Practice-oriented selection for Australian general practice; the authors state that research on the best management of benzodiazepine dependence is scarce, so practice has to be guided by general principles (p. 152).

exposure.measurement: Prescribed benzodiazepines and z-drugs, and illicit use (for example street alprazolam), as discussed; no data of the authors' own.
exposure.polysubstance: Concurrent drug misuse or dependence is named as raising the risk of harm from withdrawal, and people dependent on alcohol or other drugs as candidates for maintenance (pp. 154–155).

comparison.controls: Not applicable (no synthesis). Cited reviews compare tapering with or without psychological treatment, and medicines added to tapering.

outcomes.instruments: As discussed: withdrawal symptoms (listed in a box), long-term abstinence after stopping, relapse, DSM-5 benzodiazepine use disorder and the Severity of Dependence Scale as a screening tool (p. 152).
outcomes.validity_norms: The Severity of Dependence Scale is described as validated for community use (ref. 10, p. 152).

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited: long-term abstinence after stopping ranges from 25% at 12 months in people with complicated dependence to 80% in older adults in general practice (refs. 15, 16) (p. 154). Alprazolam dispensing in Australia rose more than eightfold over 20 years (ref. 1) (p. 152). No figures are given for how often withdrawal symptoms or seizures occur.
analysis.selective_reporting: Statements on when withdrawal and seizures occur after stopping are given without references; the half-life and equivalence table has no source.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A practice review stating, without references, that people who have taken a benzodiazepine for more than 3–4 weeks are likely to have withdrawal symptoms if it is stopped abruptly, that abrupt stopping after 1–6 months of use can cause life-threatening seizures, and that grand mal seizures can occur 1–12 days after stopping; and summarizing cited reviews on management (little robust evidence for switching to a long-acting drug; modest benefit for carbamazepine; moderate evidence for adding cognitive behavioural therapy to tapering).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary advises gradual dose reduction over weeks to lower the risk of seizures (p. 152), and the text says abrupt stopping can cause life-threatening seizures (p. 154); neither statement is referenced or quantified, and no evidence is cited that tapering lowers seizure risk compared with abrupt stopping, so the advice rests on clinical consensus rather than cited data. Elsewhere the review is candid about the evidence: it notes a paucity of research on management and that some interventions have limited supporting evidence (pp. 152, 155).

timeline.event: Cochrane review of pharmacological interventions for benzodiazepine dependence in outpatient settings (Denis et al., 2006), cited for carbamazepine's modest benefit and for gradual withdrawal in primary care.
Meta-analysis of treatment approaches for benzodiazepine discontinuation (Parr et al., 2009): gradual dose reduction with psychological treatment better than gradual reduction alone (as cited).
Descriptive review: withdrawal symptoms after 4–6 weeks of use in about 15–30% of patients; severe reactions, including seizures, described but mostly anecdotal

Cochrane review of psychosocial interventions (Darker et al., 2015): only moderate evidence that adding cognitive behavioural therapy to tapering helps; insufficient evidence on motivational interviewing (as cited).

replication.where_it_stands: The warning that abrupt stopping can cause seizures is standard clinical teaching, repeated here and in Lader (2011), but neither review gives a frequency or cites a study that measured one in people stopping therapeutic doses. Evidence on how best to stop (tapering approaches, added psychological treatment) comes from the cited Cochrane reviews and meta-analysis, not from this paper.

funding.affiliations_note: Clinical Pharmacology and Addiction Medicine, Drug Health Services, Royal Prince Alfred Hospital, and Concord Repatriation General Hospital, Sydney (p. 152). None of the 24 references are by the authors.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort or record-linkage study of people stopping long-term benzodiazepines, abruptly or by tapering, with standardized ascertainment of seizures and other severe reactions, giving absolute risks by duration of use and way of stopping; and randomized trials of tapering approaches that report seizures and other severe adverse events.

domains.note: No search or selection criteria; a short clinical review.
Some strength-of-evidence statements (no robust evidence for substitution; moderate evidence for adding CBT; flumazenil data from small groups), but none for the statements on withdrawal risk.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the references are by the authors.
Recommendations and evidence are interleaved; the statements on when withdrawal and seizures occur are uncited; the authors acknowledge the paucity of research.

domains.domain: Balance of risks of stopping against risks of continuing benzodiazepines
domains.note: Both are covered, and maintenance is offered as a harm-reduction option, but no magnitude is given for withdrawal seizures, the side a reader most needs quantified.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative clinical review (METHODS §5.3). The review is a sensible practice summary that is candid about thin evidence, but its key safety statements on withdrawal seizures are not referenced and give no frequency. Claims should cite it as Australian clinical guidance and for the management evidence it summarizes (pointing to the cited reviews), not as evidence of how often seizures follow abrupt stopping.

key_findings.finding: Anyone who has taken a benzodiazepine for longer than 3–4 weeks is likely to have withdrawal symptoms if it is stopped abruptly; the risk of dependence can be reduced by limiting prescriptions to 1–2 weeks' supply.
key_findings.locator: Prevention, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: No reference is given for either statement.

key_findings.finding: Abrupt stopping after 1–6 months of use can cause life-threatening seizures, which is why the authors advise gradual reduction.
key_findings.locator: Management › Discontinuation with the aim of abstinence, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: No reference and no frequency are given.

key_findings.finding: The box of withdrawal features lists general symptoms (headache, palpitations, sweating), muscle symptoms, neurological symptoms including confusion and delirium (particularly in older people), delusions, hallucinations and grand mal seizures 1–12 days after stopping, gastrointestinal symptoms, and psychological symptoms including rebound insomnia, anxiety and panic, perceptual distortions and depersonalization; the text adds that withdrawal symptoms may resemble the insomnia or anxiety the drug was taken for.
key_findings.locator: Box (Benzodiazepine withdrawal syndrome – clinical features); Discontinuation with the aim of abstinence, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: The box has no source.

key_findings.finding: People without unstable psychiatric or medical illness, without a history of seizures and without other drug misuse or dependence are at lower risk of harm from withdrawal; high-risk people, those with unstable medical conditions or a significant seizure history may benefit from admission to an inpatient service for stabilization or withdrawal.
key_findings.locator: Discontinuation with the aim of abstinence, 3rd paragraph (p. 154); Stabilisation and maintenance therapy, 3rd paragraph (p. 155)

key_findings.finding: Long-term abstinence after stopping varies widely, from 25% at 12 months in people with complicated dependence to 80% in older adults in general practice; lower relapse risk goes with a lower dose at the start of tapering, having already cut down substantially, less severe dependence, no previous attempts to stop, high life satisfaction and no alcohol use.
key_findings.locator: Discontinuation with the aim of abstinence, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: From refs. 15–17; the dose threshold the authors give is not recorded here (no amounts on the site).

key_findings.finding: Switching to a longer-acting benzodiazepine before tapering is a common approach and fewer people drop out of tapering on longer half-life drugs, but robust evidence supporting substitution is lacking; studies in older people found gradual withdrawal without substitution can succeed. There are no standard tapering regimens.
key_findings.locator: Management › Benzodiazepine substitution, 1st paragraph (p. 153); Discontinuation with the aim of abstinence, 5th paragraph (p. 154)

key_findings.finding: Medicines: carbamazepine has a modest benefit and pregabalin can be effective in withdrawal in people not dependent on other drugs; antidepressants and beta blockers have no proven benefit; low-dose flumazenil infusion has some supporting data from small groups, but seizures, though relatively uncommon, can occur with it, so it should be considered only in a specialized unit.
key_findings.locator: Management › Pharmacotherapy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Psychological treatment: a meta-analysis found gradual dose reduction plus psychological treatment better than gradual reduction alone; a Cochrane review found only moderate evidence that adding cognitive behavioural therapy to tapering helps and insufficient evidence on motivational interviewing; a tailored letter from the GP, standardized interviews and relaxation may reduce use.
key_findings.locator: Management › Psychotherapy, 1st paragraph (begins p. 154, continues p. 155)

key_findings.finding: For people unwilling to stop and at high risk of relapse or harm, the authors describe maintenance on a long half-life benzodiazepine as a harm-reduction strategy to prevent intoxication and withdrawal while other treatment proceeds, with referral to specialist addiction services.
key_findings.locator: Stabilisation and maintenance therapy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Context: alprazolam dispensing in Australia rose more than eightfold over 20 years; alprazolam was moved to Schedule 8 in February 2014 because of rising illicit use, and the review describes it as more toxic in overdose, with higher associated mortality, than other benzodiazepines.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 1st and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors state that research on the best management of benzodiazepine dependence is scarce, that practice is guided by general principles, and that some of the interventions they describe have limited supporting evidence.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph (p. 152); Conclusion, 2nd paragraph (p. 155)

reporting_issues.issue: The statements on when withdrawal and seizures occur after stopping (withdrawal likely after more than 3–4 weeks of use; life-threatening seizures after abrupt stopping following 1–6 months of use; grand mal seizures 1–12 days after stopping) carry no citations and no frequencies.
reporting_issues.consequence: They cannot be traced to evidence and should not be cited as evidence of how often withdrawal seizures occur.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary advises gradual dose reduction over weeks to lower the risk of seizures, but no study comparing seizure risk after tapering with abrupt stopping is cited anywhere in the review.
reporting_issues.consequence: The protective effect of tapering against seizures is asserted as consensus, not shown.

reporting_issues.issue: The table of half-lives and approximate equivalents to diazepam has no source.
reporting_issues.consequence: Its values cannot be checked; the encyclopedia does not reproduce dose equivalents in any case.

design_detail: Descriptive narrative review (published as a monograph in Addiction) by a single senior author, based on his 2010 Okey Lecture at the Institute of Psychiatry, King's College London. It covers the history, pharmacology, adverse effects, long-term use, effects in people who misuse drugs, dependence and withdrawal, abuse, extent of use and prescribing concerns for benzodiazepines and z-drugs. A search of Medline, Embase and the Cochrane databases with the search term benzodiazepine(s), alone and with terms such as dependence and abuse, and hand-searching of reference lists, found 60,000 references; the author says the review is not exhaustive. No inclusion criteria, appraisal of cited studies or quantitative synthesis; 277 numbered references, 23 of them with the author as an author (editors' count).
can_establish: What a senior researcher in the field reported in 2011 about benzodiazepine withdrawal (estimates of how often it happens, its symptoms, the severe reactions described, and the evidence on ways of stopping), and which sources each statement rests on.
cannot_establish: How often seizures or other severe reactions follow stopping, abrupt or tapered (no frequencies are given, and the review says most severe reactions are reported anecdotally); any comparison of abrupt with gradual stopping (no comparative data are presented); or the completeness of the evidence (sources were selected by the author and not appraised).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Literature search of Medline, Embase and the Cochrane databases plus hand-searching of reference lists; 60,000 references found; selection by the author (Abstract, p. 2086; Literature search, p. 2086).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; the review concentrates on adverse effects, dependence and abuse (p. 2086).
sample.selection_effects: Evidence chosen by the author. Several central withdrawal statements rest on his own earlier reviews and monograph (the 15–30% estimate, ref. 124; the observation that severity is not closely related to dose, refs. 122–123; the common and severe symptom tables, refs. 120 and 125), and the severe-symptom table also rests on a guide published by the University of Newcastle (ref. 120). The review states its own focus on adverse effects, dependence and abuse.

exposure.measurement: Varies across cited studies: prescribed benzodiazepines and z-drugs (anxiolytics and hypnotics) at therapeutic doses, and high-dose misuse, often with alcohol or opioids. Duration and amounts are reported in the review only for single studies.
exposure.polysubstance: Discussed for people who misuse benzodiazepines with alcohol, opioids or stimulants (pp. 2091–2092, 2096); not separated in the withdrawal section.

comparison.controls: Not applicable (no synthesis). Cited studies compare continuing with stopping, routine care with interventions to stop, or flumazenil with tapering or placebo.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not addressed for the cited studies; the review notes that people who take benzodiazepines have worse physical and mental health than those who do not, but that allocation to the drugs was not random (p. 2090).

outcomes.instruments: As cited: withdrawal symptoms, rebound insomnia (polysomnography), severe reactions (seizures, delirium, psychosis, depression, suicidality), abstinence after stopping, prevalence of dependence (DSM-III-R and ICD-10 criteria in one cited study).
outcomes.validity_norms: Rebound is defined as the original symptoms returning more intensely for a time, and withdrawal as new symptoms not previously experienced (p. 2092).
outcomes.operationalization: Dependence follows the WHO definition, including a physiological withdrawal state (p. 2092).

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, without intervals. Withdrawal symptoms after 4–6 weeks of use in about 15–30% of patients (ref. 124, the author's own 1998 review) (p. 2092). In a 1961 study, 11 prisoners given chlordiazepoxide at several times the usual dose for months were switched to placebo: 10 developed withdrawal reactions within 2–8 days and 2 had seizures (p. 2092). Prevalence of benzodiazepine dependence estimated at 40% in outpatients taking benzodiazepines and up to 97% in people attending self-help groups (p. 2093). About two-thirds achieve total cessation with slow tapering (uncited) (p. 2094); 60% of people who stopped after a GP's letter were still abstinent at 10 years (p. 2093). A meta-analysis of 24 intervention studies found routine care less effective than gradual dose reduction with or without psychological or pharmacological additions (p. 2094). Tolerance found in only 8% of people taking benzodiazepines in one study (p. 2101).
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection, with the review's stated focus on adverse effects, dependence and abuse; counter-views (patients finding the drugs helpful; limited population evidence of widespread dependence; prescribers' reasons) are summarized in the Concerns and Envoi sections (pp. 2100–2101). No frequency is given for any severe withdrawal reaction.

interpretation_gap.results_show: As reported: withdrawal symptoms after 4–6 weeks of use in about 15–30% of patients; rebound insomnia even after a few nights of short-acting hypnotics; symptoms appearing within two to three half-lives and usually waning within weeks or months, but fluctuating; severe reactions, including seizures, delirium, psychosis and severe depression, listed as possible after abrupt stopping and sometimes despite slow tapering, but described as mostly anecdotal, with few case series; the one quantified seizure figure is 2 of 11 people in a 1961 study at several times the usual dose. Tapering usually ends in cessation; the evidence for particular tapering methods is weak.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract presents a 'descriptive review' with a database search; the search had no selection criteria, and the 60,000 hits were not screened systematically, so the 'Methods' heading should not be read as a systematic review (p. 2086). The abstract says dependence and abuse remain serious problems and that the practical problems have been ignored by many practitioners and almost all official bodies; the body concedes that evidence of widespread dependence in population-based studies is limited and that none of the usage studies reviewed quantified tolerance or dependence (p. 2101), and that severe withdrawal reactions are largely anecdotal (p. 2092). The summary that withdrawal can be hazardous, with fits, psychosis and depression (p. 2095), states a possibility without a frequency. The conclusion that the risk–benefit ratio is positive for 2–4 weeks and unestablished beyond is offered as the author's judgment (p. 2086; p. 2102).

timeline.event: Hollister and colleagues: 11 prisoners on very high doses of chlordiazepoxide switched to placebo; 10 had withdrawal reactions within 2–8 days and 2 had seizures (as described in this review, p. 2092).
Lader's review of withdrawal after stopping hypnotics in insomnia, the source given for the 15–30% estimate (ref. 124, as cited).
Cochrane review of pharmacological interventions for benzodiazepine dependence (Denis et al., 2006), cited here for the weak evidence behind substituting diazepam.
Ten-year follow-up in the Netherlands after a GP letter: 60% of those who stopped remained abstinent (de Gier et al., 2011, as described in this review, p. 2093).

Clinical review for Australian prescribers: abrupt stopping after 1–6 months of use can cause life-threatening seizures; withdrawal seizures listed 1–12 days after stopping; neither statement referenced or quantified

replication.where_it_stands: Seizures and other severe reactions after abrupt stopping are described consistently in clinical reviews, but neither this review nor Brett and Murnion (2015) gives a frequency or cites a study that measured one in people stopping therapeutic doses; the only quantified example here is a 1961 study at several times the usual dose (2 of 11 had seizures). The figures for how often milder withdrawal occurs (15–30%) come from the author's own earlier review and need tracing to primary studies.

funding.affiliations_note: Addiction Research Centre, Institute of Psychiatry, King's College London; described in a quoted Department of Health communication as emeritus professor (p. 2091). The author reports his own research on brain imaging in long-term use and on flumazenil, states he had no contacts with a parliamentary group campaigning on tranquilliser dependence (p. 2091), and says he is encountering increasing numbers of legal actions about benzodiazepine prescribing, without describing his role in them (p. 2101). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort or record-linkage study of people stopping long-term benzodiazepines, recording how they stop (abruptly or tapered, planned or forced, for example by loss of supply), with standardized ascertainment of seizures, delirium and suicidal behaviour, to give absolute risks for each way of stopping; and randomized trials of ways of stopping that report severe adverse events.

domains.note: Databases are named, but there are no selection criteria and the 60,000 hits were not screened systematically; the author chose the evidence.
No formal appraisal; occasional caveats (severe withdrawal reactions anecdotal; cognitive studies diverse; imaging values within the normal range).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 23 of 277 references include the author, but the central withdrawal figures and symptom tables rest on his own earlier reviews and monograph.
Personal history (MRC meetings, legal actions, media campaigns) and opinion sit beside evidence; the Envoi is openly the author's view, and the anecdotal status of severe reactions is stated.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on harms and benefits of benzodiazepines
domains.note: Harms are the declared focus; benefits and the case for long-term use (patients' experience, prescribers' reasons, limited population evidence of dependence) are summarized briefly and are the under-represented side.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The review is an expert lecture turned monograph: wide-ranging, candid that its search was not exhaustive and that severe withdrawal reactions are mostly anecdotal, but unsystematic in selection and dependent on the author's own earlier syntheses for its key withdrawal figures. Claims should cite it for the description of the withdrawal syndrome, for the statement that severe reactions (including seizures) are reported but not quantified, and as a pointer to primary studies; the frequency figures should be traced to their primary sources, and nothing here measures how often seizures follow abrupt stopping.

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal symptoms can follow 4–6 weeks of use, but only in about 15–30% of patients; why some people stop after years without trouble while others suffer severely is unclear; reducing the dose, not only stopping, can bring on symptoms.
key_findings.locator: Dependence and withdrawal, 10th paragraph
key_findings.note: The 15–30% figure is cited to the author's own 1998 review of withdrawal after stopping hypnotics in insomnia (ref. 124), not to a primary study.

key_findings.finding: Severe reactions listed in Table 4 as possibly accompanying abrupt stopping, but also possible despite slow tapering, include delirium tremens, convulsions and status epilepticus that may end in death, catatonia that may result in death, depression (often severe) with possible suicidal ideation, self-harm, suicide, psychosis, mania and confusion. The author states that many of these are reported anecdotally, few case series exist and their status remains controversial; the text also says fits or a paranoid or confusional psychosis may occasionally occur. [Table 4 hedges depression as 'often severe' and suicidal ideation as 'possible'. Note should add that the depression entry cites ref. 276, a report of four cases by the author and a colleague.]
key_findings.locator: Dependence and withdrawal, 10th paragraph (p. 2092); Table 4 (p. 2093)
key_findings.note: No frequency is given for any severe reaction. Table 4 is sourced to a guide published by the University of Newcastle (ref. 120) and the author's 1984 monograph (ref. 125).

key_findings.finding: The one quantified seizure figure in the review: in a 1961 study, 11 prisoners given chlordiazepoxide at several times the usual dose for several months were switched to placebo; within 2–8 days, 10 developed depression, psychosis, agitation, insomnia, loss of appetite and nausea, and 2 had seizures.
key_findings.locator: Dependence and withdrawal, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: Very high doses in a prison setting; not representative of stopping therapeutic doses.

key_findings.finding: Whether withdrawal occurs is related to high dosage and long-term treatment, but its severity is less closely related, and severe withdrawal may occur despite slow withdrawal over months or years; with tolerance, withdrawal can also emerge in people kept on a constant dose.
key_findings.locator: Dependence and withdrawal, 8th and 9th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Supported by the author's own earlier papers (refs. 122, 123).

key_findings.finding: Rebound (the original symptoms returning more intensely) is likely when stopping hypnotic benzodiazepines, especially short-acting ones, even after only a few days or nights of use.
key_findings.locator: Dependence and withdrawal, 7th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Timing and course: symptoms appear within two to three half-lives of the drug; duration is unpredictable, but symptoms generally wane within a few weeks or months, often fluctuating markedly before resolving; higher neuroticism, lower education, lower quality of life, higher doses and low social support went with more distress. A prospective study found four patterns over 50 weeks, including worsening at the start of tapering and worsening 4 weeks after tapering ended.
key_findings.locator: Dependence and withdrawal, 11th and 12th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal symptoms may resemble the anxiety or insomnia for which the drug was first prescribed, which can lead to misdiagnosis and unnecessary dose increases.
key_findings.locator: Dependence and withdrawal, 12th paragraph (after the list of four patterns)

key_findings.finding: Prevalence of benzodiazepine dependence was estimated at 40% in outpatients taking benzodiazepines and up to 97% in people attending self-help groups (one study); elsewhere the author notes that population-based evidence of widespread dependence is limited, one study finding tolerance in only 8% of people taking benzodiazepines, and that none of the usage studies he reviewed quantified tolerance or dependence.
key_findings.locator: Dependence and withdrawal, 13th paragraph (p. 2093); Envoi, 2nd paragraph (p. 2101)

key_findings.finding: Outcomes of stopping: with slow tapering about two-thirds of patients stop completely; in a 10-year Dutch follow-up, 60% of people who stopped after a GP's letter remained abstinent; a meta-analysis of 24 intervention studies found routine care less effective than gradual dose reduction alone or combined with psychological techniques or drug substitution. Elderly people have a worse prognosis. [Source: 'gradual dose reduction' and 'pharmacological substitutions', p. 2094.]
key_findings.locator: Dependence and withdrawal, 15th paragraph (p. 2093), 18th and 21st paragraphs (p. 2094), 30th paragraph (p. 2095)
key_findings.note: The two-thirds figure carries no citation.

key_findings.finding: Evidence on how to stop is weak: substituting a long-acting benzodiazepine is widely recommended but has little evidence of efficacy; the rate of taper rests on prescribers' clinical experience, not good empirical evidence; the author's own earlier review found few objective data on the best rate or duration of withdrawal.
key_findings.locator: Dependence and withdrawal, 16th paragraph (p. 2093) and 20th paragraph (p. 2094)

key_findings.finding: Flumazenil can precipitate withdrawal (shown in a controlled study of people on long-term low doses); a series of studies found flumazenil treatment more effective than tapering or placebo, but it involves in-patient treatment, is likely to suit only a small number of severely dependent people, and large randomized trials had not been done. [The source does not call the studies small.]
key_findings.locator: Dependence and withdrawal, 27th and 28th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The author writes that withdrawal in pregnancy should never be abrupt (citing ref. 174) and that continued use into late pregnancy may cause a neonatal withdrawal syndrome in the baby that can be severe. [Attributed, so it does not read as the encyclopedia's advice.]
key_findings.locator: Dependence and withdrawal, 29th paragraph

key_findings.finding: In high-dose misuse, as with low-dose dependence, tolerance sets in rapidly and attempted stopping can bring withdrawal that is sometimes severe, with fits and psychotic reactions; high-dose use with opiates is implicated in potentially fatal overdoses; mortality seems to be increased among people who misuse benzodiazepines, though data are sparse. [Locator: Effects in drug abusers, 3rd paragraph (p. 2092); Abuse of benzodiazepines, 6th paragraph (p. 2096) and 9th paragraph (p. 2097); the overdose sentence is in the 6th paragraph, not the 7th.]
key_findings.locator: Effects in drug abusers, 3rd paragraph (p. 2092); Abuse of benzodiazepines, 7th paragraph (p. 2096); 9th paragraph (p. 2097)

key_findings.finding: The author's summary: most patients do not escalate their dose, yet physical dependence shows itself on stopping as a characteristic withdrawal syndrome; withdrawal can be hazardous, with fits, psychosis and depression; the outcome is usually favourable with tapered withdrawal. His overall conclusion is that the risk–benefit ratio is positive for most patients in the short term (2–4 weeks) but unestablished beyond that.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Conclusions (p. 2086); Dependence and withdrawal, 30th paragraph (p. 2095)

reporting_issues.issue: The estimate that withdrawal symptoms follow 4–6 weeks of use in about 15–30% of patients is presented for benzodiazepines in general but cited only to the author's 1998 review of withdrawal after stopping hypnotics in insomnia (ref. 124).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure is second-hand and may not apply to anxiolytic use or longer use; it should be traced to primary studies before being cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 (severe withdrawal symptoms, including convulsions and status epilepticus 'which may end in death') is sourced to a University of Newcastle guide and the author's 1984 monograph, gives no frequencies, and the text concedes that many entries are anecdotal.
reporting_issues.consequence: The table supports that such reactions have been described, not how often they occur.

reporting_issues.consequence: Possible citation error; the 8% figure should not be cited until its source is identified.

design_detail: Review called a scoping review by its authors (journal section: Review), by forensic toxicologists of Marche Polytechnic University, Ancona (Brunetti, Giorgetti, Tagliabracci, Busardò) and Thomas Jefferson University, Philadelphia (Huestis) (p. 1). 31 designer benzodiazepines (DBZD) were chosen from the UNODC Early Warning Advisory, the European Database on New Drugs, the US National Poison Data System and the Japanese Data Search System for NPS; PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar and Web of Science were searched to March 2021 with listed terms, with reference lists and reports of the WHO, EMCDDA, DEA and FDA; articles in English and one in Swedish; references were reviewed for relevance by one author (p. 39, 4. Materials and Methods). Of 372 potentially relevant reports, 324 were excluded; 49 reports on 12 DBZD are included, describing 254 cases reported in 2008–2021 (1 drug offence, 2 self-administration studies, 3 outpatient admissions, 44 emergency-department admissions, 63 cases of driving under the influence of drugs (DUID) and 141 deaths), tabulated with age, sex, observations, DBZD concentration or dose and co-exposures (Table 1, pp. 5–34) and summarized drug by drug (2.1–2.11, pp. 35–38). The evidence is case reports, case series and forensic series; no protocol, appraisal of the included reports, flow diagram or quantitative synthesis. Filed as a narrative review with the editors' five-domain checklist, as the round brief directs.
can_establish: Which designer benzodiazepines appeared in published reports of emergency visits, impaired driving and deaths up to March 2021 (mostly etizolam, flualprazolam, flubromazolam and phenazepam), what was recorded in those cases, and, from Table 1, which other drugs were found with them (by the editors' count, an opioid in 115 of 141 death entries).
cannot_establish: How dangerous any designer benzodiazepine is per use or compared with prescribed benzodiazepines (no denominators, no comparison); that the designer benzodiazepine caused a given death (almost all deaths involved several drugs); what blood concentration is harmful (concentrations overlapped between impaired and unimpaired drivers and between drivers and deaths); or how common use is.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review of published reports). Cases came from Finland, Germany, Japan, Norway, Poland, Sweden, the UK and the USA (p. 4, 2. Results, 3rd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Reports of emergency admissions, impaired driving or deaths in which a DBZD was the sole or explicit contributory cause of poisoning, impairment or death (p. 3, 2. Results, 1st paragraph; p. 38, 3. Discussion, 3rd paragraph); English (and one Swedish) articles, searched to March 2021. 19 of the 31 DBZD, among them bromazolam, clobromazolam, flunitrazolam and nifoxipam, had no relevant reports (p. 3).
sample.selection_effects: Case reports and forensic series select severe and detected cases; the authors note that many people exposed may never develop significant adverse events (citing Carpenter et al., 2019) and that many DBZD go undetected for lack of analytical methods or awareness (p. 39). Despite the sole-or-contributory criterion, almost every death in Table 1 involved several drugs, and some decedents appear to be listed twice under two DBZD (see reporting issues). Selection was by one author, with no stated rule for judging contribution.

exposure.measurement: Varies: DBZD detected and quantified in blood, serum, plasma, urine, oral fluid, vitreous humour or hair by LC–MS, LC–MS/MS, LC–HRMS, LC–DAD, GC–MS or GC–MS/MS (p. 4); some cases only by immunoassay screen (marked 'urine screen +') or self-report, for example two clonazolam emergency cases with the dose estimated from self-report, and flualprazolam not confirmed in three of seven emergency cases (pp. 35–36).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Mostly unknown; a few reports give self-reported amounts or a single self-administered oral dose (study conditions; not used here). Concentrations are given in Table 1 in ng/mL unless stated.
exposure.polysubstance: Co-exposures are tabulated for every case. Editors' count from Table 1 (pp. 5–34): of the 141 death entries, 115 list at least one opioid (methadone, morphine or 6-acetylmorphine, codeine, dihydrocodeine, hydrocodone, tramadol, tapentadol, fentanyl or norfentanyl, buprenorphine, brorphine, isotonitazene, oxycodone or U-47700), 2 more list loperamide or its metabolite, and 3 list no other substance. Pregabalin, gabapentin, other benzodiazepines, stimulants and alcohol are frequent.

comparison.controls: None. No comparison with prescribed benzodiazepines or with people who used DBZD without harm.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Mostly not reported in Table 1: tolerance, amount taken, medical and psychiatric history. The authors state that most patients and decedents were young people of both sexes, often with a history of substance use and mental illness (p. 4).

outcomes.instruments: Observations as reported in the sources: symptoms; impairment graded on clinical tests of impairment or standardized field sobriety tests; death scene and cause of death as given by the source; concentrations in biological samples (Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: Impairment grades (mild, moderate, considerable) and causes of death come from the source reports; the review does not say how contribution to death was judged.
outcomes.operationalization: A case enters if the DBZD was the sole or a contributory cause by the source's account; 'death' covers accidental multiple-drug toxicity, intentional poisoning, suicide and a death reported as natural.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates; counts only. Deaths by drug (text, pp. 35–38, and Table 1): phenazepam 60, flualprazolam 38, etizolam 34, flubromazolam 4, and one each for adinazolam, deschloroetizolam, diclazepam, flubromazepam and pyrazolam (editors' sum 141). Editors' count from Table 1: DUID 63 = phenazepam 19, diclazepam 13, flualprazolam 13, flubromazolam 11, etizolam 6, flubromazepam 1; emergency admissions 44 = flubromazolam 18, clonazolam 6, etizolam 4, flualprazolam 4, flubromazepam 4, diclazepam 3, phenazepam 3, 3-hydroxyphenazepam 1, meclonazepam 1. Opioid listed in 115 of 141 death entries (etizolam 29 of 34, flualprazolam 27 of 38, phenazepam 53 of 60, flubromazolam 3 of 4, other DBZD 3 of 5). Second-hand figures: UNODC, DBZD in 48% of post-mortem and 83% of DUID cases reported to it in 2019 to April 2020 (pp. 1, 3); US NFLIS seizures and undercover purchases 2391 in 2018 and 6194 in 2019 (p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: No list of excluded reports and no flow diagram; the drug-by-drug text and Table 1 disagree in places (see reporting issues).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Published reports up to March 2021 describe 141 deaths, 63 impaired drivers and 44 emergency admissions involving 12 DBZD, mostly etizolam, flualprazolam, flubromazolam and phenazepam. Emergency cases mainly showed depression of the central nervous system, some with agitation. Almost every death involved several drugs: by the editors' count, 115 of the 141 death entries list an opioid and only 3 list no other drug. Blood concentrations overlapped between impaired and unimpaired drivers and between drivers and deaths.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract opens with assertions the review does not examine: that DBZD are a 'cat-and-mouse game' between organized crime and law enforcement and are continuously modified, among other things, to increase their abuse potential (p. 1). The introduction states that, compared with classical benzodiazepines, DBZD produce strong sedation and amnesia (p. 2), citing a review of potency information and a study of prescribed benzodiazepines with opioids in people starting haemodialysis (references 41 and 42); no comparative data are presented. The statement that slow elimination of flubromazolam and phenazepam leads to accumulation in fatty tissue and delayed overdose with repeated use (p. 39) rests on two single-dose self-administration reports of other DBZD, an analysis of literature and trip reports, a forum study and a withdrawal case report (references 44, 82, 91, 152, 153). The abstract's word 'implicated' for deaths is appropriately cautious, and the Discussion says that with polydrug use a death often cannot be assigned to one drug (p. 39).

(2019): 234 single-agent designer-benzodiazepine exposures reported to US poison centres in 2014–2017, mostly etizolam and clonazolam, mainly drowsiness, 1 death; cited here for the point that many people exposed may never develop significant adverse events (p. 39, reference 154).
Bäckberg et al. (2019), Swedish STRIDA project: source of most of the flubromazolam emergency cases and of several other emergency cases in Table 1 (reference 74). Not read.
Heide et al. (2020): designer-benzodiazepine blood concentrations and impairment in Norwegian forensic cases, a source of the overlap between impaired and unimpaired drivers (reference 86). Not read.

Papsun et al. (2021) and Kriikku et al. (2020): flualprazolam in forensic and post-mortem cases in the US, Finland and Sweden, the sources of most flualprazolam deaths in Table 1 (references 101, 102). Not read.

Laing et al. (2021): at Canadian drug-checking services in 2018–2020, NPS benzodiazepines (etizolam most often) were found in samples people expected to be fentanyl or alprazolam, mostly together with fentanyl (card sc_laing_2021).
This review (published June 2021).

Morrison et al. (2025), scoping review of harm reduction for benzodiazepine use: portable drug-checking instruments detected etizolam in only part of the samples that contained it (card sc_morrison_2025).

replication.where_it_stands: This review collects the published case evidence to early 2021; its counts are of published cases, not rates. Its picture, of designer benzodiazepines found mostly with opioids and other depressants in deaths and of sedation in emergency cases, agrees with the US poison-centre series of single-agent reports (Carpenter et al., 2019) and with drug-checking findings of etizolam in samples sold as fentanyl or alprazolam (Laing et al., 2021). It does not establish the risk per use, the added risk over the other drugs present, or a harmful concentration.
