what_would_settle_it: Toxicological surveillance of all overdose deaths and emergency presentations in a region, testing every case for designer benzodiazepines with confirmed methods, so that the share involving them, the drugs found with them and outcomes with and without opioids can be estimated against a denominator; and controlled pharmacokinetic studies relating concentrations to effects and to tolerance.

domains.note: Four databases and agency reports, listed terms, searched to March 2021, English plus one Swedish article; but selection by one author, a contribution criterion that is not operationalized, no flow diagram or list of exclusions, and counts that do not add (372 − 324 ≠ 49).

No appraisal of the included reports; cases confirmed only by immunoassay or self-report sit beside quantified ones; decedents listed in two reports from the same laboratory were not recognized as the same people.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the reports in Table 1 is by the authors; their own work is cited only for background.

Motives of manufacturers, greater sedation than classical benzodiazepines and accumulation leading to delayed overdose are stated without supporting data; the Discussion does state the limits of attributing deaths and of concentrations.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on harm (severe and fatal cases against exposures without serious harm)
domains.note: By design the review collects deaths, impaired drivers and emergency cases; it notes that many exposed people may never have significant adverse events, but people who use DBZD without coming to attention are unrepresented and no denominators are given.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The search is broad and Table 1 is a useful compilation, but the included reports are not appraised, the flow does not add up, some decedents appear twice and the text and table disagree in places, so the counts are approximate. Citable for: which DBZD appear in published reports of deaths, impaired driving and emergency visits to March 2021, and that almost all the deaths involved other drugs, most an opioid (editors' count of Table 1); the overlap of concentrations between impaired and unimpaired drivers and between drivers and deaths; how DBZD are sold (counterfeit alprazolam tablets, online, several forms). Not citable for: risk per use, a comparison with prescribed benzodiazepines, causation in individual deaths, harmful concentrations, or the unsupported pharmacological statements.

key_findings.finding: Scope and flow: 31 DBZD were considered and 19 had no relevant reports; of 372 potentially relevant reports, 324 were excluded, and 49 reports on 12 DBZD were included, describing 254 cases reported between 2008 and 2021: 1 drug offence, 2 self-administration studies, 3 outpatient admissions, 44 emergency-department admissions, 63 DUID cases and 141 deaths.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1); 2. Results, 1st–2nd paragraphs (p. 3); 4. Materials and Methods (p. 39)
key_findings.note: By the editors' calculation 372 − 324 = 48, not 49 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Deaths by drug: phenazepam 60, flualprazolam 38, etizolam 34 and flubromazolam 4 (text), with one each for adinazolam, deschloroetizolam, diclazepam, flubromazepam and pyrazolam (Table 1); etizolam, flualprazolam, flubromazolam and phenazepam account for most adverse events, drug offences and deaths. The editors' sum of the drug-by-drug counts is 141.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1); 2.5 Etizolam, 2.6 Flualprazolam (p. 36); 2.8 Flubromazolam (p. 37); 2.10 Phenazepam (p. 38); single deaths in Table 1 (pp. 5–6, 24, 34)
key_findings.note: Some decedents appear twice, under two drugs, so these per-drug counts overlap (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Editors' count from Table 1: emergency admissions 44 = flubromazolam 18, clonazolam 6, etizolam 4, flualprazolam 4, flubromazepam 4, diclazepam 3, phenazepam 3, 3-hydroxyphenazepam 1 and meclonazepam 1; DUID 63 = phenazepam 19, diclazepam 13, flualprazolam 13, flubromazolam 11, etizolam 6 and flubromazepam 1.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Study column (ED and DUID rows)

key_findings.finding: Polydrug deaths, by the drug-by-drug text: of 34 etizolam deaths, 33 were recorded as accidental overdose from polydrug toxicity, in people known to use drugs or with a history of mental disorders, and 1 was a suicide; all 38 flualprazolam deaths involved multiple drugs, 36 recorded as accidental multiple-drug toxicity and 2 ruled intentional flualprazolam poisonings; of 60 phenazepam deaths, phenazepam alone was listed as the sole cause in 2 and the rest were attributed to accidental polydrug overdose.
key_findings.locator: 2.5 Etizolam and 2.6 Flualprazolam (p. 36); 2.10 Phenazepam (p. 38)
key_findings.note: Table 1 lists ethanol in one and diazepam with dihydrocodeine in the other of the two deaths attributed to phenazepam alone (p. 29), no co-exposure for two flualprazolam deaths (p. 18), and three flualprazolam entries labelled suicide (pp. 18, 21).

key_findings.finding: Editors' count from Table 1: of the 141 death entries, 115 list at least one opioid (methadone, morphine or 6-acetylmorphine, codeine, dihydrocodeine, hydrocodone, tramadol, tapentadol, fentanyl or norfentanyl, buprenorphine, brorphine, isotonitazene or U-47700) and 2 more list loperamide or its metabolite; by drug, etizolam 29 of 34, flualprazolam 27 of 38, phenazepam 53 of 60, flubromazolam 3 of 4 and the other DBZD 3 of 5. Three entries list no other substance: an etizolam suicide with only etizolam metabolites and two flualprazolam deaths; 6 of the 7 phenazepam deaths without an opioid list alcohol.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, rows with Study 'Death', Co-Exposure column
key_findings.note: Counted per table entry, so the decedents listed twice are counted twice; mitragynine (one entry) is not counted as an opioid. The authors give no such count.

key_findings.finding: Emergency cases mainly showed depression of the central nervous system: eighteen flubromazolam patients were admitted in a severe state of CNS depression with functional and motor impairment (flubromazolam the only drug detected in 16, with meclonazepam in 2); for clonazolam the primary adverse effect was CNS depression; four flubromazepam patients had agitation and delirium followed by rigidity and CNS depression; in two of three diclazepam cases there was severe agitation and disorientation, with stimulants and dissociatives also detected.
key_findings.locator: 2.2 Clonazolam and 2.4 Diclazepam (p. 35); 2.7 Flubromazepam and 2.8 Flubromazolam (p. 37)

key_findings.finding: Seizures are not counted anywhere in the review: they appear only in one pooled observation list for the Swedish flubromazolam emergency cases of reference 74 (with ataxia, coma, hallucinations, hypotension, slurred speech and unconsciousness, not given per patient) and in one etizolam outpatient with a withdrawal syndrome, slowed breathing and loss of consciousness.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Etizolam OD rows (p. 7) and Flubromazolam ED rows of reference 74 (pp. 24–25)
key_findings.note: By the editors' count, 17 patients share that observation list (13 rows on p. 24 and 4 on p. 25).

key_findings.finding: How DBZD reach people: illegally manufactured, sometimes made to look like legal medicines, and bought cheaply through online platforms; according to the UNODC, bulk materials from India and China are processed in Europe and sold as fake alprazolam or diazepam; counterfeit Xanax (alprazolam) and Erimin-5 (nimetazepam) tablets containing etizolam, flualprazolam and phenazepam were seized in the US, Australia, Singapore and Malaysia; products may contain variable amounts of active ingredient or contaminants such as novel synthetic opioids, generally without the buyer knowing; DBZD are sold online as blotters, liquids, pills, powders and tablets at low prices; etizolam and phenazepam are also diverted from countries where they are licensed medicines; etizolam, flualprazolam and flubromazolam were found in counterfeit Xanax tablets in Canada.
key_findings.locator: 1. Introduction, 3rd–4th paragraphs (p. 2, the 4th continued on p. 3); 3. Discussion, 1st–2nd paragraphs (p. 38)

key_findings.finding: Mistaken identities in the cases: seven young people were taken to emergency departments after taking a benzodiazepine they thought was alprazolam (three sedated with verbal impairment, two with CNS depression, two without symptoms; flualprazolam not confirmed in three); flubromazolam was identified in Sweden in 10 seized white tablets labelled 'XANAX' and reported to the EMCDDA in October 2014; three children were found drowsy and unsteady after eating coloured pills thought to be sweets (etizolam confirmed in one); a fatal case reported under the title 'The adulterated XANAX pill' involved etizolam with caffeine.
key_findings.locator: 2.5 Etizolam and 2.6 Flualprazolam (p. 36); 2.8 Flubromazolam (p. 37); Table 1, Etizolam death row with reference 96 (p. 13); reference 96 (p. 43)
key_findings.note: The decedent in that report (a 49-year-old man) also had ethanol (0.19 g/L) and caffeine (190,000 ng/mL) in blood, with amphetamine and cocaine in hair (Table 1, p. 13).

key_findings.finding: Most patients and decedents were young people of both sexes, often with a history of substance use and mental illness; acute intoxications and deaths were reported from Finland, Germany, Japan, Norway, Poland, Sweden, the UK and the USA.
key_findings.locator: 2. Results, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Concentrations do not separate harm from no harm: diclazepam, etizolam and phenazepam blood concentrations overlapped between impaired and unimpaired drivers, and etizolam and flualprazolam concentrations were similar in DUID cases and deaths; the authors suggest differences in tolerance after frequent use, and say concentrations are currently hard to relate to effects because few pharmacokinetic studies were performed.
key_findings.locator: 3. Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Detection limits: in many cases a DBZD will never be detected, for lack of analytical methods or awareness; newer DBZD may cross-react with common benzodiazepine immunoassays, which often cannot tell designer from prescribed benzodiazepines; metabolism to licensed benzodiazepines, the sale of metabolites of prescribed ones and the lack of confirmatory testing in health-care centres risk misinterpretation.
key_findings.locator: 3. Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state that because polypharmacy is the rule rather than the exception, causation often cannot be assigned to a single drug, and that how pathologists and toxicologists attribute the role of DBZD in deaths is largely unknown.
key_findings.locator: 3. Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Second-hand indicators: according to the UNODC, DBZD were identified in 48% of post-mortem and 83% of DUID cases reported to it between 2019 and April 2020, flualprazolam, flubromazolam and etizolam most often; US NFLIS seizures and undercover purchases of DBZD rose from 2391 in 2018 to 6194 in 2019; more than 5000 NFLIS cases of clonazolam, etizolam and flualprazolam were reported in October–December 2020; in Scotland, etizolam's numbers rose from 223 in 2016 to 752 in 2019, in a passage on drug-related deaths.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1); 1. Introduction, 4th paragraph (p. 2, continued on p. 3); 3. Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 38)
key_findings.note: Cited without denominators: the UNODC percentages are of the cases reported to UNODC, not of all deaths or drivers, and the review does not say which cases these were; the unit of the Scottish figures (deaths implicating etizolam) is implied, not stated.

key_findings.finding: Control: clonazolam, diclazepam, etizolam, flualprazolam and flubromazolam were placed in Schedule IV of the 1971 Convention in 2020–2021; international control of flualprazolam, phenazepam, flubromazolam and etizolam came two, five, seven and nine years after formal notification.
key_findings.locator: 1. Introduction, 5th paragraph (p. 3); 3. Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 38)

key_findings.finding: Etizolam is a licensed medicine in India, Italy, Japan and Korea for short-term treatment of insomnia, anxiety and panic, not elsewhere; three people with psychiatric disorders came to outpatient care for etizolam detoxification after tolerance and withdrawal (one with seizures); clonazolam is described, citing one case report, as 'insanely powerful', with strong sedation and amnesia at very small oral amounts and easy accidental overdose.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Etizolam OD rows (p. 7); 2.2 Clonazolam (p. 35); 2.5 Etizolam (p. 36)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that slow elimination and active metabolites of some DBZD (flubromazolam, phenazepam) lead to accumulation in fatty tissue, which can cause a delayed overdose with repeated use.
key_findings.locator: 3. Discussion, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Supported only by two single-dose self-administration reports of other DBZD, a literature and trip-report analysis, a forum study and a withdrawal case report (references 44, 82, 91, 152, 153); an untested statement.

reporting_issues.issue: Flow arithmetic: 372 potentially relevant reports less 324 excluded leaves 48, but 49 reports are said to be included; no list of excluded reports or flow diagram is given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The selection cannot be reproduced; minor for the counts of cases.

reporting_issues.issue: Probable double listing: four death entries appear twice in Table 1, once under etizolam and once under another DBZD, with the same age and several identical concentrations but other details differing. (a) A 39-year-old man with etizolam 4, diazepam 68, cocaine 184, cocaethylene 22, quetiapine 16 and mirtazapine 121 (p. 12, etizolam; p. 26, flubromazolam): morphine 1076 against 1149, and the etizolam entry omits flubromazolam 70. (b) A 49-year-old man with etizolam 1.5, diazepam 89, methadone 685 and mirtazapine 12 (p. 11; p. 26): flubromazepam 33 in one entry and flubromazolam 33 in the other, morphine 44 against 73, pregabalin 38,100 against 38.1. (c) A 33-year-old with etizolam 14, flubromazolam 1, cocaine 46, clozapine 2060, norclozapine 1629 and procyclidine 186 (p. 13; p. 27): male in one entry and female in the other, morphine 56 against 91, lamotrigine and gabapentin differing by a factor of one thousand. (d) A 37-year-old man with etizolam 85, methadone 189 and pregabalin 8500 (p. 10, etizolam; p. 22, flualprazolam 14.1).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 141 deaths probably count at least four people twice (by the editors' calculation, 137 or fewer distinct decedents), and per-drug death counts overlap. The duplicated etizolam, flubromazolam and flualprazolam rows sit under references 95, 108 and 103, which share authors (Hikin, Smith and Morley among them); the PDF does not name their laboratory. Cite 'about 140 deaths in published reports'.

reporting_issues.issue: Text against Table 1: the text says all 38 flualprazolam deaths involved multiple drugs and 2 were intentional flualprazolam poisonings, while Table 1 lists two flualprazolam deaths with no co-exposure under 'Suspected overdose, Multiple drugs' and three entries labelled suicide; the text counts seven flualprazolam emergency patients and three etizolam emergency admissions, while Table 1 lists four of each.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the table appears to hold only the analytically confirmed emergency cases, which is not said.

reporting_issues.issue: The two deaths in which phenazepam alone was listed as the cause ('Phenazepam intoxication') list ethanol 0.22 g/L in one and diazepam and dihydrocodeine in the other.
reporting_issues.consequence: Even these were not phenazepam-only exposures; do not cite them as deaths from a designer benzodiazepine alone.

reporting_issues.issue: Implausible or unit-inconsistent values in Table 1: pregabalin 6500000 (p. 9); pregabalin 38.1, gabapentin 24.6 and lamotrigine 5.8 in entries whose apparent duplicates give 38,100, 24,600 and 5800, although the footnote says ng/mL unless specified (pp. 26–27); two identical phenazepam death entries (blood 80; etizolam and diazepam screen positive; morphine 590) on p. 31.
reporting_issues.consequence: Concentrations in Table 1 should not be cited without the primary report; the identical entries may be one more duplicate.

reporting_issues.issue: Ambiguous etizolam passage: after accounting for all 34 deaths, the text refers to 'these nine cases' (references 92, 95, 97), with etizolam 1–237 ng/mL and etizolam not listed as the cause; the nine are not introduced, and the one case from reference 92 in Table 1 has 264 ng/mL.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether nine further deaths exist outside the 34, or are part of them, cannot be told.

reporting_issues.issue: Slips: in the flubromazepam section, flubromazolam and U-47700 are said to be the listed cause of the one death, while Table 1 and the cited report concern flubromazepam with U-47700; the deschloroetizolam self-administration is cited to reference 79 (an analytical-method paper) in the text but to reference 82 in Table 1; the list of DBZD without reports names difludiazepam, while the search terms name norflunitrazepam instead.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor.

design_detail: Retrospective descriptive analysis of coded, de-identified records of the US National Poison Data System (NPDS), the database of reports made by members of the public and health-care providers to member centres of the American Association of Poison Control Centers (AAPCC), coded by Specialists in Poison Information and uploaded in near real time (PDF pp. 2–3, Methods, 1st paragraph). Cases: intentional exposures to a single substance among 11 coded designer benzodiazepines (adinazolam, clonazolam, cloniprazepam, diclazepam, etizolam, flubromazepam, flubromazolam, meclonazepam, nifoxipam, norflurazepam, pyrazolam), 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2017, any route; accidental ingestions and exposures to more than one substance excluded. Etizolam had a specific code from 2007; codes for the other agents were added only in 2016, and designer benzodiazepines without a specific code could not be retrieved. Only clinical effects coded 'Related' and therapies coded 'Performed' or 'Recommended and Performed' were counted; narrative case text was not requested (PDF p. 3, Methods, 2nd–3rd paragraphs). Descriptive summaries by agent (etizolam, clonazolam, flubromazolam columns) and year; state counts normalized per million population with 2014 Census estimates (PDF p. 3, Methods, 4th paragraph). The authors call it a retrospective cohort study; there is no comparison group, so it is filed as a registry (poison-centre records) and appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for record studies.
can_establish: How many intentional single-agent exposures to 11 coded designer benzodiazepines were reported to US poison centres in 2014–2017 (234; 26 in 2014 to 112 in 2017; etizolam 162, clonazolam 50), who the reported people were (median age 25, 86% male), and which clinical effects, treatments, levels of care, graded outcomes and durations were coded for them.
cannot_establish: That the coded drug was the drug taken (no laboratory confirmation, and products came from unregulated sources); what happens when designer benzodiazepines are taken with other drugs (multi-agent exposures, about half of all reports, were excluded); how often use leads to harm or how common use is (only reported exposures, no denominator of people who use them); whether reports rose because use rose (codes for agents other than etizolam began only in 2016); or the effect of any amount (quantities were not recorded).

sample.recruitment: Records, not recruited people: all reports to AAPCC member poison centres coded with one of the 11 designer-benzodiazepine codes in 2014–2017; callers were members of the public and health-care providers (PDF p. 2, Methods, 1st paragraph). Exposures occurred in 40 states (18 in 2014 and in 2015, 30 in 2016, 36 in 2017); California had the most (21), and Vermont and Minnesota the most per population (PDF p. 3, Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 2, PDF p. 4).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: intentional exposures to one substance among the 11 coded agents, any route, 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2017. Excluded: accidental ingestions and exposures to more than one substance (PDF p. 3, Methods, 2nd paragraph). Of 474 designer-benzodiazepine exposures reported, 234 met the criteria (PDF p. 3, Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Median age 25 years (range 13–63); 201 men (86%) and 32 women (14%), sex missing for 1 (editors' count, 201 + 32 = 233). NPDS reason category: 'Abuse' 138 (59%), suspected suicide 42 (18%), 'Misuse' 31 (13%), intentional–unknown 23 (10%); the paper does not define the categories. Exposure acute 158 (77%), acute-on-chronic 29 (14%), chronic 19 (9%), among the 206 with a coded exposure type (editors' sum) (Table 1, PDF p. 4). Route: ingestion 224 (95%), inhalation/nasal 5 (2%), parenteral 5 (2.1%) (PDF p. 3, Results, 2nd paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable to records. Denominators differ by field because of unknown values, without explanation: exposure type known for 206, disposition for 224, outcome percentages computed on about 229, duration known for 178 (editors' calculations from Tables 1 and 4, PDF pp. 4–5).
sample.selection_effects: Only exposures someone reported to a poison centre enter the data; the authors expect that people without significant symptoms were not reported, so totals are under-counted and severity over-represented (PDF p. 6, Discussion, last paragraph). Excluding multi-agent exposures (about half of all reports) leaves out combinations with opioids, alcohol or other drugs, whose outcomes were not analysed (PDF pp. 4–5, Discussion, 2nd paragraph). Only agents with a specific code could be retrieved: a death after flubromazolam, coded under the generic code 'Benzodiazepine' in the 2016 NPDS annual report, is missing (PDF p. 4, Discussion, 1st paragraph). Codes for agents other than etizolam began in 2016, so 2014–2015 counts are etizolam only (Table 2, PDF p. 4).

exposure.measurement: The substance as reported by the caller and coded by poison-centre staff. Forensic testing to confirm the exposure is not routinely performed (PDF p. 3, Methods, 1st paragraph, continued from PDF p. 2). The authors state that exposures may be misclassified because people likely bought an illegal drug from an unregulated source, that standard immunoassays may show a positive benzodiazepine result, and that confirmatory testing is unavailable to most US clinicians (PDF p. 5, Discussion, 4th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Amounts not recorded (for the one death, the quantity was unknown). Route: ingestion 95%, inhalation/nasal 2%, parenteral 2.1%. Exposure acute in 77%, acute-on-chronic in 14%, chronic in 9% of those with a coded type.
exposure.polysubstance: Exposures involving more than one substance were excluded: 240 of the 474 reports were not included (editors' calculation; the paper says 234, or 49%, involved multiple agents). Whether people in the included group had also taken substances that were not reported cannot be known from these data.

comparison.controls: None. Descriptive series; the only contrasts are between agents (etizolam, clonazolam and flubromazolam columns in Tables 1, 3 and 4) and between years (Table 2).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not recorded or not requested: other substances taken (beyond the exclusion), amounts, tolerance, psychiatric and medical history, laboratory confirmation and the narrative of each case (PDF p. 3, Methods, 3rd paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: NPDS coded fields: clinical effects coded 'Related'; therapies coded 'Performed' or 'Recommended and Performed'; level of care (treated/evaluated and released; admitted to non-critical care, critical care or a psychiatric facility; lost to follow-up or left against medical advice); NPDS medical outcome (no, minor, moderate or major effect; death); duration of effects (PDF p. 3, Methods, 3rd paragraph; Tables 3 and 4, PDF p. 5).
outcomes.validity_norms: NPDS coding is standardized (details in the NPDS annual report, cited on PDF p. 3). The authors note that effects may go unrecognized by the treating clinician, therapies may be reported incompletely and coding errors occur (PDF p. 6, Discussion, last paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Severe effects' are not defined beyond the NPDS grades (major effect, death) and single effects such as coma, respiratory depression or arrest, cardiac arrest and intubation.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: counts and percentages only, no statistical tests or confidence intervals.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes; descriptive counts. Reports per year 26, 30, 66 and 112 (2014–2017), a 330% increase; etizolam alone 26, 30, 46, 60 (Table 2, PDF p. 4), a 131% increase (editors' calculation). Of 234: drowsiness/lethargy 152 (65%), slurred speech 40 (17%), coma 10 (4%); IV fluids 74 (32%), naloxone 17 (7%), intubation 7 (3%) (Table 3, PDF p. 5). Of 224 with a known disposition: critical care 49 (22%), non-critical admission 31 (14%) (Table 4, PDF p. 5). Major effect 9 (4%), death 1 (0.4%) (Table 4). Duration under 24 h in 85% of the 178 with a known duration (Table 4; PDF p. 4, Results, 3rd paragraph). The per-million rates in the text cannot be reproduced (see reporting issues).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration mentioned. The Emory University Institutional Review Board judged the project exempt; the investigators did not interact with subjects and the data held no protected health information (PDF p. 3, Methods, 5th paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only the ten most common effects and therapies are tabulated (Table 3), so respiratory depression (3%), respiratory arrest and cardiac arrest (0.4% each) appear only in the text. Table 4 is titled 'Known case outcomes' but its outcome percentages do not add to 100, and the missing categories are not shown. Multi-agent exposures, about half of all reports, were not collected or analysed.
analysis.power: Not applicable. With 234 reports, single rare outcomes (1 death) are imprecise.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Reports to US poison centres of intentional single-agent exposures to coded designer benzodiazepines rose from 26 in 2014 to 112 in 2017 (etizolam alone, the only agent coded throughout, 26 to 60). In the 234 reports, drowsiness or lethargy was coded in 65% and slurred speech in 17%; of those with a known disposition, 22% were admitted to critical care; 3% were intubated, 4% had a major effect and 1 person died; effects lasted under 24 h in 85% of those with a known duration.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions say the incidence of exposures is rising and will likely keep rising (PDF pp. 2, 6). The counts are reports, not incidence, and part of the 330% rise spans the codes added in 2016, which the authors acknowledge as reporting bias (PDF p. 6). The conclusion that severe effects, including death, are infrequent (PDF p. 6) fits the single-agent reports (major effect 4%, death 0.4%), but it leaves out the half of reports with other agents, sits beside 22% critical-care admissions, and the authors themselves expect severity to be over-reported (PDF p. 6). The statement that effects fit a sedative-hypnotic toxidrome (PDF p. 2) holds for most coded effects; agitation/irritability (9% in Table 3, 14% in the text) and tachycardia (9%) are not discussed.

timeline.event: Case report cited by the authors: flubromazolam as a new life-threatening designer benzodiazepine (Łukasik-Głębocka et al., 2016). Not read.
This study published online (print issue 2019).

Bäckberg et al. (2019), Swedish STRIDA project, as summarized by Brunetti et al. (2021): 18 emergency patients with flubromazolam, admitted in a severe state of central nervous system depression. Not read.

Brunetti et al. (2021), review of published case reports to March 2021: 44 emergency admissions, 63 impaired drivers and 141 deaths with designer benzodiazepines, mainly central nervous system depression in emergency cases and other drugs, mostly opioids, in almost all deaths; it cites this study (card sc_brunetti_2021).

Laing et al. (2021): at Canadian drug-checking services in 2018–2020, NPS benzodiazepines (etizolam most often) were found in samples people expected to be fentanyl or alprazolam, mostly together with fentanyl (card sc_laing_2021).

replication.where_it_stands: The sedative picture of single-agent reports (drowsiness, slurred speech, ataxia, mostly short-lived) agrees with the later review of case reports (Brunetti et al., 2021), in which deaths almost always involved other drugs. Drug-checking data (Laing et al., 2021) show why the coded identity is uncertain: designer benzodiazepines are often in products sold as something else. No study read for this card gives the risk of harm per use or outcomes for designer benzodiazepines combined with opioids against either alone.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflict of interest (PDF p. 6, Disclosure statement).
funding.affiliations_note: All authors are at the Georgia Poison Center, Atlanta; Kazzi and Gittinger also at the Department of Emergency Medicine, Emory University School of Medicine (PDF p. 2).

what_would_settle_it: Poison-centre or emergency-department surveillance in which the drug is confirmed by laboratory testing of the patient's own samples, multi-agent exposures are analysed alongside single-agent ones (for example designer benzodiazepine with and without opioids), and all designer benzodiazepines are coded from the start, so that the severity and its change over time can be estimated without misclassification or coding artefacts.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: NPDS covers reports to all AAPCC member centres, the right frame for reported exposures; it misses exposures never reported and agents without a specific code (other agents than etizolam only from 2016).
A census of coded intentional single-agent reports, but half of all reports (multi-agent) were excluded and the flow from 474 to 234 is not fully accounted for.
234 reports suffice to describe common effects; rare outcomes (1 death) are imprecise.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Age, sex, reason, exposure type, route and state; no amounts, histories or narrative case details.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Denominators differ by field (206, 224, about 229, 178) without explanation; the missing outcome categories are not shown.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: The agent is the caller's report as coded, without laboratory confirmation; the authors state that products from unregulated sources may have held other compounds.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: Standard NPDS coding by poison specialists, but voluntary reporting, possible unrecognized effects and coding errors, and a coding change in 2016.
Descriptive counts are appropriate, but the per-million rates are wrong, several text percentages contradict the tables, and no intervals are given.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response managed appropriately
domains.note: Reporting to poison centres is voluntary; the share of exposures reported is unknown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As a national census of reported, coded single-agent exposures, the counts and the tabulated effects, treatments, levels of care and outcomes are usable with their denominators, and the authors state the main limits themselves. The risk is moderate for that description; as evidence of what a named designer benzodiazepine does, it is high, because the agent was not confirmed, reports favour symptomatic cases, multi-agent exposures were excluded and codes changed in 2016. Citable for: reported single-agent exposures rising from 26 to 112 a year (etizolam alone 26 to 60), mostly etizolam and clonazolam; drowsiness or lethargy in 65%; 22% of those with a known disposition admitted to critical care; 3% intubated; 1 death in 234; effects under 24 h in 85% of known durations. Not citable for: incidence or rates per population, risk per use, outcomes of combinations with opioids or alcohol, or the effect of any particular drug or amount.

key_findings.finding: 474 designer-benzodiazepine exposures were reported to US poison centres in 2014–2017; 234 intentional single-agent exposures met the criteria, rising every year from 26 in 2014 to 112 in 2017, a 330% increase; exposures came from 40 states.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (PDF p. 2); Results, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3); Table 2 and its footnote (PDF p. 4)
key_findings.note: The 2014–2015 counts are etizolam only, because codes for the other agents were added in 2016 (Table 2 footnote, PDF p. 4); etizolam alone rose from 26 to 60 (by the editors' calculation, an increase of 131%).

key_findings.finding: By agent: etizolam 162 (69%), clonazolam 50 (21%), flubromazolam 13, diclazepam 4, flubromazepam 3, meclonazepam 1, norflurazepam 1; etizolam was the most common in every year (26, 30, 46 and 60 reports).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3); Table 2 (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: The people reported: median age 25 years (range 13–63), 86% male; NPDS reason category 'Abuse' 59%, suspected suicide 18%, 'Misuse' 13%, intentional–unknown 10%; route ingestion 224 (95%), inhalation/nasal 5 (2%), parenteral 5 (2.1%).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st–2nd paragraphs (PDF p. 3); Table 1 (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Clinical effects coded among the 234: drowsiness/lethargy 152 (65%), slurred speech 40 (17%), confusion 32 (14%), agitated/irritable 22 (9%), ataxia 21 (9%), tachycardia 20 (9%), hypotension 19 (8%), coma 10 (4%), bradycardia 9 (4%); the text adds respiratory depression (3%), respiratory arrest (0.4%) and cardiac arrest (0.4%).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 3); Table 3 (PDF p. 5)
key_findings.note: The text gives coma as 8% and agitation/irritability as 14% (PDF p. 3), against 10 (4%) and 22 (9%) in Table 3; the table's counts are used here.

key_findings.finding: Treatments recorded: IV fluids 74 (32%), naloxone 17 (7%), oxygen 17 (7%), benzodiazepines 15 (6%), other sedation 13 (6%), flumazenil 9 (4%), intubation 7 (3%), ventilator 5 (2%).
key_findings.locator: Table 3, Therapy rows; also Results, 2nd paragraph (PDF pp. 3–4)

key_findings.finding: Level of care: treated/evaluated and released 92 (41%), admitted to non-critical care 31 (14%), admitted to critical care 49 (22%), admitted to a psychiatric facility 36 (16%), lost to follow-up or left against medical advice 16 (7%); the percentages are of those with a known disposition (editors' sum of these rows: 224).
key_findings.locator: Table 4, Disposition rows; also Results, 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 4) and Abstract (PDF p. 2)
key_findings.note: The abstract's 36% of cases admitted to hospital and 22% to intensive care combine the non-critical and critical-care admissions (editors' calculation: 31 + 49 of 224); psychiatric admissions are counted separately.

key_findings.finding: Graded outcome: no effect 18 (8%), minor effect 101 (44%), moderate effect 76 (33%), major effect 9 (4%), death 1 (0.4%); 77% had minor or moderate effects. The one death was a 29-year-old man after an intentional ingestion of etizolam coded as abuse; the quantity was unknown.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 4); Table 4, Outcome rows (PDF p. 5)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: the outcome percentages fit a denominator of about 229 reports, not the 205 with a shown outcome or all 234; the remaining categories are not shown.

key_findings.finding: Duration of effects: under 2 h 8, 2–8 h 57, 8–24 h 86 (together under 24 h in 85% of the cases with clinical effects and a known duration), 24 h to 3 days 19 (11%), 3 days to 1 week 7 (4%), over 1 week 1 (0.6%). One etizolam case had symptoms beyond 1 month, with agitation, confusion, drowsiness, electrolyte abnormalities and kidney failure needing haemodialysis.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 4); Table 4, Duration of Effect rows (PDF p. 5)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: the duration rows add to 178; 151 of 178 under 24 h is 84.8%.

key_findings.finding: A death outside the data: a 24-year-old man who died after an acute flubromazolam exposure, described in the 2016 NPDS annual report, was coded under the generic 'Benzodiazepine' code and so was not retrieved.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Multi-agent exposures (given as 234 of 474, 49%) were neither collected nor analysed; the authors suggest that future studies compare the severity of co-ingestions with single-agent ingestions.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 4, continued on PDF p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Flumazenil was given to 9 people, none of whom had a seizure; 2 of the 9 reported an acute-on-chronic or chronic exposure. The authors judge the numbers too small to conclude on its safety after designer-benzodiazepine exposure.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The agent was not confirmed: forensic testing is not routinely performed in NPDS; because products likely came from unregulated sources, people may have taken compounds other than those coded; standard immunoassays may show a positive benzodiazepine result, and confirmatory testing is unavailable to most US clinicians.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph (continued on PDF p. 3); Discussion, 4th paragraph (PDF p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Because reporting is voluntary and people without significant symptoms are unlikely to be reported, the authors expect the total number of exposures to be under-counted and the severity of symptoms over-reported.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, last paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The yearly counts are given as 5 per million population (26 in 2014) and 20 per million (112 in 2017), while the state map's scale of cumulative exposures per million runs only from 0 to 5 (Figure 2). By the editors' calculation the two rates imply populations of about 5.2 and 5.6 million, far below that of the United States.
reporting_issues.consequence: The per-million figures cannot be national rates and should not be cited; how they were computed is not stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives coma as 8% and agitation/irritability as 14% (Results, 2nd paragraph), while Table 3 gives 10 (4%) and 22 (9%) of 234.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the table's counts; the text percentages are those of the table's hypotension (8%) and confusion (14%) rows, not of coma or agitation.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives 48/234 subjects as 23% and flumazenil as given to 9 subjects (3%), against 4% for flumazenil in the Results and Table 3. Editors' calculation: 48 of 234 is 20.5%, and 23% is 48 of the 206 with a coded exposure type; 9 of 234 is 3.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; percentages in the text use varying denominators and rounding.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4, titled 'Known case outcomes', has outcome percentages that fall well short of the whole, and some percentages in Tables 3 and 4 are mis-rounded (etizolam bradycardia and intubation printed as 4 (3%), antiemetics as 3 (1%); durations under 2 h as 8 (5%)). Editors' calculation: the outcome percentages add to 89.4% and fit a denominator of about 229 (etizolam about 158, clonazolam 49) rather than the 205 with a shown outcome; disposition percentages are of 224 and durations of 178; 4 of 162 is 2.5%, 3 of 162 is 1.9%, 8 of 178 is 4.5%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite outcome shares with the caveat that the denominators are partly unexplained; counts are more reliable than percentages.

reporting_issues.issue: The number 234 is used both for the included single-agent exposures (Results) and for the exposures involving multiple agents, said to be 49% of 474 (Discussion); 474 − 234 − 234 leaves 6 reports unaccounted for (editors' calculation), presumably excluded single-agent accidental exposures, which the paper does not say.
reporting_issues.consequence: The flow of reports is not fully reported; the share of multi-agent reports is about half either way.

reporting_issues.issue: The 330% increase compares 2014, when only etizolam had a code, with 2017, after codes for the other agents were added in 2016; the abstract presents it as a rise in the incidence of exposures.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the etizolam-only series (26 to 60) for a like-for-like rise in reports; neither series measures incidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The design is called a retrospective cohort study (Methods, 1st paragraph), but there is no comparison group or follow-up of an exposed population; it is a descriptive series of poison-centre records.
reporting_issues.consequence: No comparative or causal inference is possible from this design.

design_detail: Placebo-controlled within-person choice study in three groups of paid volunteers aged 21–35 without a history of drug abuse: 12 controls, 11 with anxious mood (high scores on anxiety scales, no DSM-III anxiety disorder) and 13 with DSM-III generalized anxiety disorder. Each person took part in three experiments in counterbalanced order: 5 mg d,l-amphetamine, 5 mg diazepam and 10 mg diazepam, each against placebo. An experiment had four sampling sessions (drug twice and placebo twice, each in a capsule of its own colour) and then five choice sessions in which the person chose which colour to take; three sessions a week, capsule taken between 9 and 10 am, after which participants went about their day. Outcomes: number of drug choices (0–5), liking, identification of the capsule, and mood questionnaires (POMS, ARCI) before and 1, 3 and 6 hours after the capsule.
can_establish: Whether, in these young volunteers without a history of drug abuse, people with high anxiety or generalized anxiety disorder chose a single morning dose of 5 or 10 mg diazepam over placebo more often than people without anxiety, and how those doses changed mood ratings over six hours.
cannot_establish: Whether anxious people are at risk of dependence (only single doses on separate days were given, although the abstract draws a conclusion about dependence); how people with heavy drinking or other drug use histories respond (a history of drug abuse was an exclusion criterion); how people seeking treatment, people in acute distress, or people who can choose when and how much to take respond; or what happens at other doses, times of day or settings.

sample.recruitment: Advertisements in the student newspaper, posters on campus and word of mouth; the advertisements for the anxious groups asked whether the reader felt anxious, tense or nervous. The study was presented as research, not treatment, with monetary benefits only (p. 534, Subjects and Methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph). Screening: interview with psychiatric profile, medical and drug-use history, an electrocardiogram and a cardiologist's examination, anxiety questionnaires and a psychiatric interview by a trained professional (2nd paragraph). University of Chicago.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 21–35. Excluded: serious medical problems, a history of drug abuse, or a history of major depression, bipolar disorder or schizophrenia (DSM-III). Controls: no DSM-III axis I disorder, TMAS 18 or less, STAI 37 or less, and HSCL anxiety and depression scores below the 90th percentile of a community sample. Generalized anxiety disorder group: DSM-III criteria met. Anxious mood group: high scores on two of the three anxiety scales without meeting criteria for any DSM-III anxiety disorder (p. 534, Subjects, 3rd paragraph and group definitions).
sample.demographics: Mean age 26 (controls), 27 (anxious mood) and 27 (generalized anxiety disorder); men/women 6/6, 4/7 and 4/9. Mean STAI 29.9, 44.7 and 49.1; TMAS 9.2, 22.8 and 27.1; HSCL anxiety 0.15, 0.58 and 0.95; HSCL depression 0.20, 0.63 and 0.95 (both anxious groups above controls, P<.01; the generalized anxiety group above the anxious mood group on both HSCL scales, P<.05) (Table 1, p. 535). Drug use, numbers in the same order (Table 2, p. 536): more than 7 drinks a week now 3, 4 and 2; marijuana never used 0, 3 and 4; stimulants ever used 5, 7 and 7; hallucinogens ever used 2, 4 and 3; recreational tranquilizer use ever 1, 2 and 3; prescribed tranquilizers at least once 3, 0 and 5.
sample.attrition: 42 started and 36 completed. Six did not complete (three controls, three from the anxious mood group): five for personal reasons unrelated to the study and one control because of the sedative effects of diazepam. Only completers are analysed (p. 535, Results › Subject Characteristics, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Young, paid volunteers from a university community, told that the study offered no treatment. A history of drug abuse or of major depression excluded people, so the people most often asking how benzodiazepines feel (people who drink heavily or use other drugs) are absent by design, although 9 of 36 reported drinking more than 7 drinks a week. Anxious people who answer research advertisements may differ from patients seeking treatment; the authors note that acutely distressed people, or people less disturbed by sedation, might respond differently (p. 541, Comment, 13th paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Given by the investigators: diazepam (Valium) or amphetamine sulfate (Benzedrine) tablets inside opaque size-00 gelatin capsules filled with dextrose; placebo capsules held dextrose only. Each person's drug and placebo had one consistent colour each, with colours assigned randomly across people (p. 534, Procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Capsules were swallowed in the laboratory; choices were recorded at each choice session.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: one oral capsule of 5 mg d,l-amphetamine, 5 mg diazepam, 10 mg diazepam or placebo, taken between 9 and 10 am; three sessions a week for three weeks per experiment (four sampling and five choice sessions), three experiments in all. Participants were told that any dose would be within the daily therapeutic range (p. 534, Instructions and Consent; Procedure).
exposure.polysubstance: Participants agreed to take no other drugs, apart from their usual amounts of coffee and cigarettes, from 12 hours before to 6 hours after each capsule (p. 534, Instructions and Consent); no verification is reported. Background alcohol and drug use is in Table 2 (p. 536); choice was not analysed by drinking or drug history.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Self-reported 12-hour abstinence from other drugs except caffeine and tobacco; not biologically verified.

comparison.controls: Within each person: placebo (dextrose capsules) against each active drug. Between groups: controls against the two anxious groups. 5 mg d,l-amphetamine served as a comparison drug that normal volunteers had chosen over placebo in earlier studies (p. 534, Introduction, 6th paragraph).
comparison.matching: Similar mean ages (26–27). Women were 50%, 64% and 69% of the three groups, which the authors call closely matched on sex, without a test (p. 535). Not matched on depression scores, which were higher in both anxious groups; the authors discuss this as a possible confound (p. 540, Comment, 8th paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the within-person diazepam–placebo comparison. For the group comparison, expectations, personality and earlier benzodiazepine experience were not analysed as moderators.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Among the 12 controls, 3 drank more than 7 drinks a week, all had used marijuana and 5 had used stimulants (Table 2, p. 536). More people in the anxious groups had never used marijuana (7 of 24 against 0 of 12; P<.05 by chi-square) (p. 536, Results › Subject Characteristics, 2nd paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Number of drug choices in five choice sessions (main outcome); a questionnaire at hour 6 on liking (from disliked a lot to liked a lot), on what the capsule was thought to be (stimulant, tranquilizer or placebo) and on unusual reactions; an experimental version of the Profile of Mood States (72 adjectives, eight subscales plus derived Arousal and Positive Mood) and a 49-item Addiction Research Center Inventory (A and BG stimulant-like scales, MBG euphoria, PCAG sedation, LSD dysphoria), completed before the capsule and 1, 3 and 6 hours after (pp. 534–535, Procedure; Subjective Effects).
outcomes.validity_norms: POMS and ARCI are described as sensitive to psychotropic drugs (p. 534). Group HSCL anxiety scores were compared with 95th percentiles of 0.43 (men) and 0.75 (women) in a large California sample (p. 540, Comment, 6th paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Preference = number of drug choices (0–5), grouped as 0–1, 2–3 and 4–5 for logit models; amphetamine group means were also tested against chance (2.5) by one-sample t tests (p. 540, Comment, 10th paragraph). Relative liking = mean drug against mean placebo liking over the four sampling sessions, people with equal scores omitted (p. 535, Data Analysis).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 18 outcome measures (choices, liking, identification, 10 POMS subscales and 5 ARCI scales) in each of three experiments; 45 multivariate repeated-measures analyses with several effects each, of which only effects at P<.05 are shown (Table 6, p. 538).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Participants were told only that any capsule might hold a stimulant, a minor tranquilizer or a placebo (p. 534, Instructions and Consent). The paper does not say whether the staff handing out capsules knew their contents. Ratings were self-completed, mostly outside the laboratory.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes or confidence intervals; logit models and multivariate analyses of variance. Choice (Table 3, p. 536; numbers of people with 0–1, 2–3 and 4–5 drug choices, all 36): amphetamine 6, 10 and 20; 5 mg diazepam 21, 7 and 8; 10 mg diazepam 27, 4 and 5. Linear trend across the categories: amphetamine z=2.3, P<.02 (towards drug); 5 mg diazepam z=−2.2, P<.03 and 10 mg diazepam z=−3.0, P<.004 (towards placebo); no group differences in any experiment. Mean amphetamine choices 4.0 (controls), 3.1 (anxious mood) and 2.9 (generalized anxiety) of 5; only the controls chose amphetamine more often than chance (p. 540). Editors' reading of Figure 1 (p. 536), checked against the axis ticks (the amphetamine bars reproduce the printed means, and each reading lies within the range Table 3 allows): mean diazepam choices about 2.1, 1.1 and 2.4 (5 mg) and 1.3, 0.4 and 1.5 (10 mg) of 5 for controls, anxious mood and generalized anxiety. Editors' calculation: if each choice were a coin toss, 19% of people would land in 0–1 and 19% in 4–5; observed 58% and 22% (5 mg diazepam), 75% and 14% (10 mg diazepam), 17% and 56% (amphetamine). Identification (Table 4, p. 537): 10 mg diazepam called a tranquilizer by 30 of the 36 who gave a consistent answer, 5 mg by 18 of 32; amphetamine called a stimulant by 14 and placebo by 14 of 33. Liking and choice (Table 5, p. 537): choice × liking interactions z=2.03, P<.04 (amphetamine) and z=2.51, P<.02 (5 mg diazepam); at 10 mg a main effect towards placebo, z=2.63, P<.01, and interaction z=1.81, P<.06.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only significant (P<.05) subjective-effect results are tabulated (Table 6); main effects of hour are left out; numerical means are given only for POMS Anxiety and Anger (Table 7); drug-minus-placebo time courses appear only as figures without numbers (Figures 2–4). Diazepam choice means are given only in a figure.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 11–13 people per group, the study had little power to detect group differences in choice or group × drug interactions in mood; the authors' statement that diazepam affected all groups alike rests on non-significant interactions.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 36 young volunteers without a history of drug abuse, no group preferred a single morning dose of 5 or 10 mg diazepam to placebo: most people chose the placebo capsule more often (21 of 36 chose diazepam at most once in five sessions at 5 mg, 27 of 36 at 10 mg), and people with anxious mood or generalized anxiety disorder chose no differently from controls. Diazepam lowered anxiety ratings and raised sedation, confusion and (at 10 mg) fatigue ratings; at 10 mg it also lowered elation, friendliness and positive mood and raised depression and dysphoria scores, with no change on the euphoria scale. Most people could tell that 10 mg diazepam was a tranquilizer. 5 mg amphetamine was chosen more often than placebo overall, significantly above chance in the controls only.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the results suggest "individuals with high anxiety are not at greater risk for dependence on antianxiety drugs" (p. 533), and the Comment that anxiety level itself may not raise the risk of dependence on diazepam (p. 541, 13th paragraph). Dependence was not studied: the evidence is preference for single morning doses of one drug at two doses, taken in a research setting by volunteers told not to expect treatment. The authors themselves list conditions their test did not cover (acute distress, people less bothered by sedation, expectations, extensive previous sedative or alcohol use) (p. 541). Similarity of effects across groups is inferred from non-significant interactions in groups of 11–13. The Comment's statement that diazepam had no effect on Elation or Positive Mood (p. 540, 4th paragraph) conflicts with the significant decreases at 10 mg in the Results and Table 6 (p. 538), and its statement that the groups did not differ in lifetime drug use (p. 540, 8th paragraph) with the marijuana difference reported in the Results (p. 536).

timeline.event: Johanson and Uhlenhuth: normal volunteers chose placebo over 5 and 10 mg diazepam (diazepam on 28% and 27% of choice sessions) and 5 mg d-amphetamine over placebo (76%) (as described by this paper, p. 534, and by Griffiths & Weerts, 1997, Table 3).
Griffiths and colleagues: people with a history of sedative abuse chose diazepam over placebo, but pentobarbital over diazepam (as described by this paper, p. 534).
This study: anxious volunteers and controls without drug-abuse histories did not prefer single morning doses of diazepam to placebo.
McCracken and colleagues: 14 anxious people seeking treatment chose 10 mg diazepam on 37% of choice sessions (as summarized by Griffiths & Weerts, 1997, Table 3).

Chutuape and de Wit: in evening sessions in which people decided capsule by capsule whether to take more, 22 anxious volunteers chose diazepam on 65% of sessions against 45% for 23 controls (marginal, P=0.06) (as summarized by Griffiths & Weerts, 1997).
Roache and colleagues: of four women with generalized anxiety disorder choosing capsules as needed over several weeks, three chose diazepam exclusively (as summarized by Griffiths & Weerts, 1997).

Review: benzodiazepines are chosen over placebo by people with drug-use histories and by moderate drinkers, rarely by other volunteers; in anxious people the result depends on whether they control timing and amount.

replication.where_it_stands: Under this single-morning-dose procedure anxious volunteers did not prefer diazepam, and a later study of anxious people seeking treatment found the same (McCracken et al., 1990, as summarized by Griffiths & Weerts, 1997). Studies that let anxious people decide when and how much to take found a preference (Chutuape & de Wit, 1995; Roache et al., 1996 and 1997, as summarized by the same review). Those primary papers have not been read for this card.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse grant DA 02812 awarded to Dr Uhlenhuth (p. 541).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Drug Abuse Research Center, Department of Psychiatry, University of Chicago; presented in part at the meeting of the Committee on Problems of Drug Dependence, Toronto, June 1982 (p. 533). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A within-person choice study with randomized order and blinded staff in people with anxiety disorders recruited from clinics as well as by advertisement, comparing a fixed single dose with participant-controlled dosing, with groups defined by drinking and other drug use and enough people to test group × drug interactions; and prospective follow-up of people starting prescribed benzodiazepines, to see whether laboratory preference predicts later long-term or non-medical use.

domains.note: The three experiments were given in counterbalanced order and drug-first or placebo-first sampling was split between about half of the participants; capsule colours were assigned at random. How people were allocated to orders is not described (p. 534, Procedure).

Sessions were on separate days and effects were expected to be gone by hour 6 (p. 535), but experience in one experiment (for example knowing that a capsule could hold a tranquilizer) could shape choices in the next; experiment order was not analysed.

Participants were told only the three possible kinds of capsule; staff blinding is not stated. Capsules were swallowed in the laboratory. Abstinence from other drugs was self-reported. That most people could recognize 10 mg diazepam is part of what a choice procedure tests, not a deviation.

6 of 42 (14%) did not complete and only completers were analysed; one control left because of diazepam's sedative effects. That person would probably have chosen placebo, so the omission works against, not for, the main finding.
Choice is a recorded behaviour; mood ratings are self-reports by people not told the capsule's contents (though many could identify diazepam).
No protocol; only significant subjective effects are tabulated, main effects of hour are omitted, means are given for two POMS subscales only, and diazepam choice means only in a figure.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: RoB 2 applied to the within-person comparison of diazepam with placebo. The finding that these volunteers did not prefer diazepam holds at both doses and in all three groups and rests on a behavioural outcome, so the concerns (undescribed counterbalancing, staff blinding not stated, completer analysis, selective tabulation of mood results) are unlikely to reverse it. The comparison between anxious and non-anxious groups is not randomized and has little power. Cite the paper for what single morning doses of 5 and 10 mg diazepam did in young volunteers without drug-abuse histories, including people with generalized anxiety disorder: they did not prefer it to placebo, and it calmed and sedated without euphoria. Do not cite it for dependence risk, for people with heavy drinking or other drug use, or for dosing that people control themselves.

key_findings.finding: Design: 42 volunteers aged 21–35 without a history of drug abuse started and 36 completed (12 controls, 11 with anxious mood, 13 with DSM-III generalized anxiety disorder). Each took part in three experiments (5 mg d,l-amphetamine, 5 mg diazepam and 10 mg diazepam, each against placebo), each with four sampling and five choice sessions, three a week, the capsule taken between 9 and 10 am, after which participants left the laboratory.
key_findings.locator: Subjects and Methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph; Procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 534); Results › Subject Characteristics, 1st paragraph (p. 535)

key_findings.finding: No group preferred diazepam to placebo. Numbers of people choosing diazepam on 0–1, 2–3 and 4–5 of five occasions (all 36): 21, 7 and 8 at 5 mg; 27, 4 and 5 at 10 mg (at 10 mg: controls 9, 1 and 2; anxious mood 10, 1 and 0; generalized anxiety 8, 2 and 3). The proportions fell across the categories (z=−2.2, P<.03 at 5 mg; z=−3.0, P<.004 at 10 mg), and the three groups did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Results › Number of Drug Choices, 2nd, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 3

key_findings.finding: 5 mg d,l-amphetamine was chosen more often than placebo (0–1, 2–3 and 4–5 choices: 6, 10 and 20 people; positive trend z=2.3, P<.02), with no group difference. Mean amphetamine choices were 4.0 (controls), 3.1 (anxious mood) and 2.9 (generalized anxiety) of 5; in one-sample t tests against chance (2.5), only the controls chose it significantly more often.
key_findings.locator: Results › Number of Drug Choices, 1st paragraph; Table 3 (p. 536); Comment, 10th paragraph (p. 540)

key_findings.finding: Figure 1 shows mean numbers of drug choices (of 5) by group: amphetamine above 2.5 in all groups, diazepam below 2.5 in all groups at both doses, lowest in the anxious mood group.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1
key_findings.note: Editors' reading at 300 dpi against the axis ticks (the amphetamine bars reproduce the printed means of 4.0, 3.1 and 2.9): diazepam about 2.1, 1.1 and 2.4 at 5 mg and 1.3, 0.4 and 1.5 at 10 mg for controls, anxious mood and generalized anxiety; each reading lies within the range implied by Table 3. Weighted by group size, about 38% (5 mg) and 22% (10 mg) of choices went to diazepam (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Most participants could tell diazepam: 10 mg was called a tranquilizer by 30 of the 36 who gave a consistent answer (all 13 in the generalized anxiety group), 5 mg by 18 of 32; amphetamine was called a stimulant by 14 and placebo by 14 of 33; placebo was named correctly by 25 of 35, 25 of 32 and 30 of 35 in the three experiments. Group did not affect identification.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Identification, 1st–4th paragraphs (p. 536, continuing on p. 537); Table 4 (p. 537)

key_findings.finding: Liking and choosing went together, but differently by drug: people who liked amphetamine more than placebo mostly chose it (interaction z=2.03, P<.04); people who liked placebo more than 5 mg diazepam very often chose placebo, while those who liked diazepam more were only slightly more likely to choose it (z=2.51, P<.02); at 10 mg, people chose placebo more often whichever they had liked more (z=2.63, P<.01). Group made no difference.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Choice and Drug Liking, 1st–3rd paragraphs; Table 5
key_findings.note: Table 5 excludes people with equal liking for drug and placebo; by its footnote, 10 of 15 such people chose amphetamine three to five times, 6 of 11 chose 5 mg diazepam three to five times and 1 of 5 chose 10 mg diazepam three to five times. The amphetamine counts add to 37, one more than the 36 analysed (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: How diazepam felt on the questionnaires (alike in all groups; no group × drug interactions): at both doses anxiety, vigor, arousal and stimulant-like (BG) scores fell at 1 and/or 3 hours, and confusion and sedation (PCAG) scores rose; 10 mg also raised fatigue. At 10 mg, depression and dysphoria (LSD scale) scores were higher and friendliness, elation and positive mood lower on drug days than on placebo days. Diazepam did not change the euphoria (MBG) scale.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective Effects, Diazepam Experiments paragraphs (p. 538); Table 6 (p. 538); Figures 3 and 4 (p. 539)

key_findings.finding: Mean POMS Anxiety over all sessions was lower in controls than in both anxious groups in every experiment: 0.47, 0.70 and 0.77 (amphetamine); 0.44, 0.88 and 0.73 (5 mg diazepam); 0.38, 0.80 and 0.70 (10 mg diazepam) for controls, anxious mood and generalized anxiety. The anxious mood group also had higher Anger in the 5 mg experiment (0.328 against 0.067 in controls).
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective Effects, Amphetamine Experiment and Diazepam Experiments paragraphs; Table 7

key_findings.finding: 5 mg d,l-amphetamine raised the euphoria (MBG) scale relative to placebo at 1, 3 and 6 hours (drug × hour, P<.001) and raised the BG and A scales, but changed no POMS subscale, anxiety included.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective Effects, Amphetamine Experiment paragraph; Table 6; Figure 2 (p. 538); Comment, 2nd paragraph (p. 539)

key_findings.finding: Background alcohol and drug use (numbers of controls, anxious mood and generalized anxiety participants): more than 7 drinks a week 3, 4 and 2; marijuana never used 0, 3 and 4; stimulants ever used 5, 7 and 7; recreational tranquilizer use ever 1, 2 and 3; prescribed tranquilizers at least once 3, 0 and 5. Choice was not analysed by drinking or drug history.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subject Characteristics, 2nd paragraph (p. 535, continuing on p. 536); Table 2 (p. 536)

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that the anxious participants neither chose nor liked diazepam more than controls although it lowered their anxiety scores, that the results do not support the idea that highly anxious people take benzodiazepines to self-medicate, and that other anxious subgroups (people in acute distress, people less disturbed by sedation) or people with extensive previous sedative or alcohol use might respond differently.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 3rd paragraph (p. 540); 13th and 15th paragraphs (p. 541)

key_findings.finding: Background cited in the introduction: in a large US national survey (Mellinger and colleagues), 11% of adults had taken a prescribed antianxiety drug (usually a benzodiazepine) in the past year, 67% of them for less than a month, and only 1.6% of all adults surveyed (aged 18 to 79) had used one daily for as long as a year.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures from Mellinger, Balter and Uhlenhuth (1984), not this study's data.

reporting_issues.issue: The legend of Figure 3 says the panels show amphetamine minus placebo, but the panels are headed 5 mg and 10 mg diazepam and show diazepam's effects on POMS subscales.
reporting_issues.consequence: A labelling error; the text (p. 538) makes clear that Figure 3 shows diazepam.

reporting_issues.issue: The Comment states that diazepam had no effect on the Elation or Positive Mood scales, whereas the Results and Table 6 report significant main effects of 10 mg diazepam on both (lower on drug sessions, P=.003 each).
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should follow the Results: at 10 mg diazepam lowered elation and positive mood; at no dose did it raise them.

reporting_issues.issue: The Comment says the groups did not differ in lifetime drug use, while the Results report significantly more people who had never used marijuana in the anxious groups (7 of 24 against 0 of 12, P<.05). The Comment also says people with dysthymic disorder were excluded, which the Methods do not list.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor internal inconsistencies about who was studied.

reporting_issues.issue: The marijuana difference rests on a chi-square test with expected counts of 2.3 and 4.7 in two cells; Fisher's exact test on the same counts gives a two-sided P of about 0.07 (editors' calculation; the uncorrected chi-square gives about 0.04).
reporting_issues.consequence: The groups may not have differed in marijuana use at the stated level; this affects the description of the sample, not the choice results.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 5 and its footnote, the amphetamine experiment accounts for 37 people (22 in the table and 15 with equal liking), one more than the 36 analysed, and the 10 mg diazepam experiment for 35 (30 and 5), one fewer.
reporting_issues.consequence: A transcription or tabulation slip of one person in each experiment; the direction of the liking–choice findings is not affected.

reporting_issues.issue: Three printed P values are smaller than the two-sided values their z statistics imply: z=2.3 with P<.02 (two-sided about .021), z=2.03 with P<.04 (about .042) and z=1.81 with P<.06 (about .070) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Consistent with one-sided tests or loose rounding; the diazepam choice trends (z=−2.2 and −3.0) are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper does not say whether the staff who gave the capsules knew their contents; a later review lists all its human studies, this one included, as double-blind (Griffiths & Weerts, 1997, Table 3 footnote a).
reporting_issues.consequence: Blinding of staff cannot be confirmed from this paper.
