design_detail: Narrative review by two authors from the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, based on the first author's Solvay Duphar Award lecture to the American Psychological Association. Part 1 summarizes the prevalence and problems of long-term and recreational benzodiazepine use, mostly from second-hand US survey figures from about 1990–1995. Part 2 reviews benzodiazepine self-administration: Table 2 lists 13 human laboratory studies in people with histories of drug abuse, Table 3 lists 17 in people without, and Tables 4–6 list 24 intravenous, 21 intragastric and 18 oral animal studies. No search strategy, inclusion criteria, quality appraisal or pooling; some significance labels in Table 3 were derived by the reviewers with one-tailed tests.
can_establish: What the human laboratory and animal self-administration studies that the authors selected (published up to 1997) showed about when benzodiazepines are chosen over placebo: almost always by people with drug-use histories, rarely by volunteers without such histories, and in some studies of moderate drinkers, anxious people and people with insomnia, depending on the procedure.
cannot_establish: Whether the summarized picture is complete or unbiased (no systematic search or appraisal); how large the differences are (no pooling); whether drug history itself, rather than the much higher doses and different procedures used with drug-experienced participants, explains why they chose benzodiazepines; or whether choosing a benzodiazepine in the laboratory predicts long-term or non-medical use outside it.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Human studies as tabulated (Tables 2–3, pp. 8–13): men with histories of drug abuse (12 of 13 studies; one also included women), 2 to 16 per study; and people without such histories: healthy volunteers (7 to 43 per study), light and moderate social drinkers (12 to 55), people with and without a first-degree relative with alcoholism (14 and 13), anxious volunteers and people with generalized anxiety or panic disorder (4 to 22), people seeking treatment for anxiety (14), and people with insomnia (7 to 9 per group, or three groups of 8).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated. Two choice studies comparing triazolam with zopiclone in alcohol-treatment inpatients were left out because they lacked a placebo and did not replicate (Table 2 footnote b, p. 9); eight oral rat studies that did not clearly show reinforcement were left out of Table 6 for brevity (Table 6 footnote a, p. 27).
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors'. 11 of the 13 studies in Table 2 have the first author as a co-author, 12 of the 17 in Table 3 have de Wit or Johanson among their authors, and several animal studies are the authors' own. The drug-experienced samples are small and almost all male. The prevalence and sales figures come from a 1990 survey cited through another review (Balter, cited by Woods et al. 1992) and rest on an assumption that dose does not change with duration of use (p. 2).

exposure.measurement: Varies by cited study: drug given by the investigators, orally and double-blind in all human studies except two early studies without blinding or placebo (Table 2 comments and footnote a; Table 3 footnote a). Procedures: sampling sessions followed by mutually exclusive drug-or-placebo choices; self-administration earned by work such as riding an exercise bicycle; drug-versus-money multiple-choice questionnaires.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as tabulated: people with drug-abuse histories were given much higher doses than volunteers without such histories (for example diazepam 40–400 mg in three studies in Table 2, against 2–20 mg as single doses, or several 4 mg capsules spread over an evening or a day, in Table 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed for the cited studies, except that moderate drinkers in the diazepam-choice studies reported more weekly marijuana use than light drinkers, and that people who chose diazepam in a pooled analysis of choice studies reported more current marijuana use and more lifetime stimulant use (p. 14).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported for the cited studies.

comparison.controls: Placebo in most human studies; other drugs as comparators (pentobarbital, chlorpromazine, buspirone, abecarnil, d-amphetamine, ethanol, oxazepam); comparisons between populations (drug history, drinking level, anxiety, insomnia) made across studies.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable; comparisons between populations are made across studies that differ in dose, procedure, setting and laboratory, which the review does not take into account.

outcomes.instruments: Cited outcomes: percentage of choice sessions on which drug was chosen over placebo; percentage of a group choosing drug on more than half of occasions; number of doses self-administered; money value at which drug and money were chosen equally; subjective ratings (liking, euphoria, ARCI scales) as indirect measures; in animals, injections or deliveries per day against vehicle.
outcomes.validity_norms: A drug chosen or self-administered more than placebo is called a reinforcer, and one chosen significantly less often a punisher (p. 13). Significance labels in Table 3 come from the original articles (footnote b) or from the reviewers' own one-tailed tests against 50% chance: a z test on the proportion of people choosing drug on more than half of occasions, or a t test on mean percentage drug choice (footnotes c and d, p. 13).
outcomes.operationalization: Drug reinforcement is defined as a drug increasing the likelihood of the behaviour that produces it through its action on the brain, whatever the stated motive: taking it to feel good, to avoid anxiety or to avoid withdrawal all count (p. 6, Drug reinforcement as a mechanism..., 1st paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis); the reviewers' own re-tests are one-tailed and uncorrected.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, no pooling. Long-term use (1990 US survey, as cited, p. 2): past-year use 8.3% for anxiolytics and 2.5% for hypnotics; 36% of people who used an anxiolytic in the past year (3% of adults) used it for 4 or more months in a row (25% continuously), and 23% of people using a hypnotic did (14% continuously). Human laboratory studies (Tables 2–3): in people with drug-abuse histories, diazepam was chosen over placebo on every occasion and oxazepam on 79% (16 men), and lorazepam over buspirone by 7 of 8. In volunteers without such histories, diazepam was chosen on 28% and 27% of choice sessions at 5 and 10 mg against 76% for 5 mg d-amphetamine (10 people); lorazepam 2 mg on 16% and flurazepam 30 mg on 20% (12 each); 10 mg diazepam on 25%, 32% and 38% in three groups; diazepam on 33% (43 people) and on 38% and 48% in people without and with a family history of alcoholism. Moderate against light social drinkers (about 12 against 4 drinks a week): diazepam choice 100% against 66%, 73% against 40%, and 64% in moderate drinkers against 27% for buspirone. Anxious people: 37% (14 seeking treatment); 65% against 45% in controls (P=0.06); 3 of 4 and 11 of 14 showing clear preference when taking capsules as needed. Insomnia: triazolam chosen on 86% of nights under mutually exclusive choice. Context: 8 of 8 chose triazolam before relaxation, 0 of 8 before a vigilance task. Speed of onset: faster-onset conditions (peaks at 61 against 220 minutes for diazepam; 1.7 against 9.2 hours for immediate- against extended-release alprazolam) gave more liking or euphoria and more impairment. Animals: benzodiazepines intermediate between barbiturates and buspirone or chlorpromazine; 12 of 12 baboons self-injected triazolam; 8 of 18 tabulated oral studies negative.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. Eight oral rat studies that did not clearly show reinforcement are named only in a footnote (p. 27), and the text's eight of 18 negative oral studies (p. 28) leaves them out. The human tables do include negative studies. Long-term efficacy is discussed briefly and without a search.
analysis.power: Not applicable; most cited human studies had 4 to 16 participants per group, which the review does not weigh.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In the studies tabulated, men with drug-abuse histories almost always chose benzodiazepines over placebo (13 studies of 2 to 16 people), while volunteers without such histories usually chose placebo as often or more often (16% to 38% drug choice in single-dose studies). Moderate social drinkers chose diazepam in three studies while light drinkers did not; anxious people chose it in three of five studies, those letting them control timing and amount; people with insomnia chose triazolam under mutually exclusive choice (86% of nights) but not under optional self-administration. Faster-onset conditions produced more euphoria and more impairment, and in one study of eight people the task that followed (relaxation or vigilance) decided which drug was chosen.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says benzodiazepines function as reinforcers in people with anxiety, insomnia and moderate drinking histories (p. 1), more firmly than the body's mixed results allow (two of five anxiety studies negative and one marginal; insomnia only under one procedure, pp. 14–15). The thesis that reinforcement is the main mechanism of both recreational and long-term therapeutic use is framed as a hypothesis, but the definition used counts symptom relief and avoidance of withdrawal as reinforcement, so long-term therapeutic use is classed as reinforcement almost by definition (pp. 6–7). The contrast between people with and without drug histories is also a contrast in dose and procedure, which the review does not discuss. The long-term use and sales figures are second-hand. The conclusion that there is "little empirical justification for most long-term benzodiazepine use" (p. 30) rests on an absence of efficacy evidence summarized without a search, while the introduction calls benzodiazepines extremely safe and effective (p. 1). The review is cautious about moderate drinkers (implications unclear, pp. 30–31) and flags its comparisons across studies as not tested prospectively.

timeline.event: Johanson and Uhlenhuth: 10 healthy volunteers chose placebo over 5 and 10 mg diazepam and 5 mg d-amphetamine over placebo (as summarized in Table 3).
Griffiths and colleagues: 16 men with drug-abuse histories chose diazepam over placebo on every occasion and oxazepam on 79% (as summarized in Table 2).
Anxious volunteers and controls without drug-abuse histories did not prefer single morning doses of diazepam to placebo
de Wit, Pierri and Johanson: diazepam chosen by moderate but not light social drinkers (as summarized in Table 3); later found again by de Wit and Doty (1994) and Evans and colleagues (1996).
Roache and colleagues: 3 of 4 women with generalized anxiety disorder taking capsules as needed chose diazepam exclusively (as summarized in Table 3).

Roache and colleagues (in press when the review was written): 11 of 14 people with generalized anxiety or panic disorder showed clear alprazolam preference; Roehrs and colleagues: people with insomnia chose triazolam on 86% of nights under mutually exclusive choice (as summarized in Table 3).

replication.where_it_stands: A comprehensive narrative account, up to 1997, of who chooses benzodiazepines over placebo in the laboratory. Its key distinction (people with drug-use histories and moderate drinkers against other volunteers) rests mostly on studies from two laboratories, and the review cites no study that compared people with and without drug-use histories at the same doses. Later laboratory work is not among the papers read for this card.

Much of the human evidence in drug-experienced people (11 of 13 studies in Table 2) and several animal studies are the authors' own. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: Human laboratory studies comparing people with defined histories (none, light and moderate drinking, recreational drug use, anxiety disorders, insomnia) under the same doses and procedures (fixed single dose against self-paced dosing, daytime against evening), with pre-registered analyses; prospective cohorts linking laboratory preference to later long-term or non-medical use; and a systematic review with appraisal of the choice studies, to show how robust the effect of drug history is.

domains.note: No databases, dates, search terms or criteria; called comprehensive, but negative oral rat studies appear only in a footnote and two zopiclone studies were excluded by the authors' judgement.
Table comments flag missing placebo control and blinding, and the reviewers re-tested some results, but there is no formal appraisal; small samples are not weighed, and the re-tests are one-tailed.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 11 of 13 studies in drug-experienced people (Table 2) and several animal studies are co-authored by the first author; the studies in people without drug histories come mostly from another group.

Comparisons across studies are flagged as not tested prospectively and the mechanism is framed as a hypothesis, but the abstract states reinforcement in anxious people and people with insomnia more firmly than the mixed results support.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against benzodiazepine reinforcement
domains.note: Negative human studies are tabulated and discussed; the under-represented side is the negative animal evidence (eight oral rat studies left out of Table 6) and, for long-term use, evidence of benefit, argued from its absence without a search.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The review is detailed and mostly careful, but its selection is unsystematic, it relies heavily on the authors' laboratory for drug-experienced participants, and its comparisons between populations are not controlled for dose or procedure. Cite it for the pattern of laboratory findings on who chooses benzodiazepines over placebo and as a pointer to the primary studies, whose figures here are second-hand; cite the 1990 prevalence and sales estimates only as the review's citation of another source.

key_findings.finding: From a 1990 US general-population survey (as cited): past-year use was 8.3% for anxiolytics and 2.5% for hypnotics; 36% of people who used an anxiolytic in the past year (3% of adults) had used it for 4 or more consecutive months (25% continuously), and 23% of people using a hypnotic had (14% continuously). The authors estimate that almost 90% of anxiolytics and more than 80% of hypnotics sold in 1990 were taken by people reporting daily use for 4 months or longer.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1); Long-term use of benzodiazepines: prevalence, problems, and vulnerable populations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 2); Figure 1 (p. 3)
key_findings.note: Second-hand: the survey is cited as Balter, cited by Woods et al. (1992), and the sales estimate assumes that dose does not change with duration of use.

key_findings.finding: Problems of long-term use as summarized: complete tolerance does not develop to the memory-impairing effects, even after years; falls and hip fractures are associated with use in older people; evidence on accidents is largely inconclusive except for higher rates in older drivers; brain damage is questionable; the share of long-term patients at risk of withdrawal has been estimated at 50% but is hard to assess.
key_findings.locator: Memory impairment (pp. 3–4); Risks of accidents; Risk of falls or hip fractures among the elderly; Withdrawal syndrome after termination of chronic use; Brain damage (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Heavier use in some groups, as cited: in the US in 1991 people aged 65 or older were 13% of the population but received 27% of benzodiazepine anxiolytic and 38% of hypnotic prescriptions; 13% to 22% of people aged 65 or older in community and outpatient surveys reported current or recent use, and long-term use reached 35% to 77% in some surveys of older people in institutions; as many as 40% to 60% of people with chronic pain used benzodiazepines; rates of use above 30% are not uncommon in studies of people with alcohol problems.
key_findings.locator: Overuse among the elderly, 1st paragraph (pp. 4–5); Overuse among chronic pain patients; Overuse by alcoholics (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Non-medical use, as cited: 7.1% of the US high-school class of 1995 reported non-medical use of tranquilizers (mostly benzodiazepines; cited to a 1995 press release), and about half of people who used them reported usually getting high from them (cited to an earlier survey report, Johnston et al. 1993, so the two figures do not describe the same people); most non-medical use is oral and alongside other drugs, with high rates among people using heroin and people on methadone maintenance. [The card's 'about half of those' joined two different surveys, against its own RI6.]
key_findings.locator: Recreational benzodiazepine abuse..., 1st and 2nd paragraphs (the section after Overuse by alcoholics)

key_findings.finding: The authors judge diazepam to have greater abuse liability than many other benzodiazepines, and oxazepam and halazepam relatively low, from laboratory studies in drug-experienced people, interviews, clinicians' judgement and epidemiological data; flunitrazepam was popular among people using opioids, with over 4000 US law-enforcement encounters in 37 states between 1994 and March 1997.
key_findings.locator: Recreational benzodiazepine abuse..., 4th and 5th paragraphs (p. 6, left column, the 5th continuing in the right column)

key_findings.finding: Drug reinforcement is defined without regard to motive: taking a benzodiazepine to feel good, to avoid anxiety or to avoid withdrawal symptoms all count as reinforcement. The authors speculate that a more general reinforcement mechanism may explain much of long-term use better than therapeutic effect alone, since many long-term patients report trouble controlling use and taking it to avoid withdrawal, and long-term efficacy has not been clearly shown. [The paper calls this speculation and says 'may provide a more satisfactory explanation for much of' long-term use, not that it 'best explains most'.]
key_findings.locator: Drug reinforcement as a mechanism engendering both chronic long-term use and recreational abuse of benzodiazepines, 1st paragraph (p. 6) and 3rd paragraph (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: The authors judge the person's history to be the most important single determinant of whether a benzodiazepine works as a reinforcer. Studies in people with histories of drug abuse almost always found that it did (Table 2, 13 studies; for example diazepam chosen over placebo on every occasion and oxazepam on 79% in 16 men), with higher doses usually more reinforcing, benzodiazepines less reinforcing than pentobarbital and more than chlorpromazine, buspirone or abecarnil, and diazepam more than oxazepam. Lorazepam was chosen over buspirone by 7 of 8, but with no placebo the table calls it unclear whether lorazepam was a reinforcer; four of the 13 studies had no placebo comparison (editors' count).
key_findings.locator: Reinforcing effects of benzodiazepines in humans › Benzodiazepines are reinforcers in subjects with histories of drug abuse..., 1st paragraph (p. 7, continuing on p. 13); Table 2 (pp. 8–9)

key_findings.finding: In volunteers without drug-use histories who were light drinkers without anxiety or insomnia, benzodiazepines were consistently not chosen over placebo, and in several studies they were chosen less often: diazepam on 28% and 27% of choice sessions at 5 and 10 mg against 76% for 5 mg d-amphetamine (10 people); lorazepam 2 mg on 16% and flurazepam 30 mg on 20% (12 people each); 10 mg diazepam on 25%, 32% and 38% in three groups; diazepam on 33% (43 people). Amphetamine was chosen under the same conditions.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (pp. 10–11); Benzodiazepines are reinforcers in subjects with histories of drug abuse..., 2nd paragraph (p. 13)

key_findings.finding: Moderate social drinkers chose diazepam over placebo in three studies, light drinkers did not (in the two de Wit studies, means of 12 and 4 drinks a week): diazepam choice 100% against 66% (de Wit et al. 1989; 12 and 18 people), 73% against 40% (de Wit & Doty 1994; 14 and 13 people; the difference was significant), and 64% in the 30 moderate drinkers tested with diazepam, against 27% choice of buspirone in the 25 tested with it (Evans et al. 1996). The percentage of moderate drinkers who preferred diazepam (2 or 3 of 3 choices) was 100%, about 71% and about 70%. About 30% of 20- to 40-year-olds meet or exceed the criteria for moderate drinking. [The drinking means are given for the two de Wit studies only, p. 13.]
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (pp. 10–12); Benzodiazepines are reinforcers in subjects with histories of moderate social alcohol drinking, 1st paragraph (p. 13, continuing on p. 14); Figure 2 (p. 14)
key_findings.note: Figure 2 values for de Wit & Doty (1994) and Evans et al. (1996) are the editors' reading at 300 dpi against the axis (about 71% against 29% and 70% against 30%). The 66% for light drinkers in de Wit et al. (1989) was a non-significant tendency towards diazepam.

key_findings.finding: The authors suggest, noting that it was not investigated prospectively, that occasional recreational drug use not meeting criteria for abuse or dependence may be associated with choosing diazepam: in both studies contrasting moderate with light drinkers, the moderate drinkers used marijuana weekly significantly more often (weekly use averaged 26% among moderate drinkers in the three studies), and in a pooled analysis of earlier diazepam choice studies in volunteers screened to exclude substance abuse or dependence, people who chose diazepam reported more current marijuana use and more lifetime stimulant use (Chutuape & de Wit 1994).
key_findings.locator: Benzodiazepines are reinforcers in subjects with histories of moderate social alcohol drinking, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The authors flag this as not investigated prospectively.

key_findings.finding: In anxious people, five double-blind studies gave mixed results. In the two using a single morning dose diazepam was not a reinforcer and placebo was preferred (Table 3 marks diazepam as a punisher in both; de Wit et al. 1986; McCracken et al. 1990: 14 people seeking treatment chose 10 mg diazepam on 37% of sessions). Three that let people control timing and total amount found preference: 22 anxious volunteers chose diazepam on 65% of evening sessions against 45% for 23 controls (marginal, P=0.06) and took more capsules (Chutuape & de Wit 1995); 3 of 4 women with generalized anxiety disorder chose diazepam exclusively, and 11 of 14 people with generalized anxiety or panic disorder showed clear alprazolam preference, mostly at low, stable rates, when taking capsules as needed for 4 weeks (Roache et al. 1996, 1997).
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (pp. 10–13); Benzodiazepines can function as reinforcers in anxious subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 14, continuing on p. 15); Figure 3 (p. 14)

key_findings.finding: In people with insomnia, triazolam was chosen on 86% of nights when a mutually exclusive choice with placebo was offered (three groups of 8; Roehrs et al. 1997); under optional self-administration, placebo was taken on more than 60% of nights, not different from triazolam (capsules taken on 77% of nights in the triazolam condition and 80% in the placebo condition) (Roehrs et al. 1992, 1996, 1997).
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (pp. 11–12); Benzodiazepines can function as reinforcers in insomniac subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 15)

key_findings.finding: Context decided choice in one study of eight people with drug-abuse histories: all 8 chose triazolam before a relaxation task and none before a vigilance task, while 7 of 8 chose d-amphetamine before the vigilance task (Silverman et al. 1994).
key_findings.locator: Contextual determinants of benzodiazepine reinforcing effects..., 2nd paragraph (p. 15, continuing on p. 16); Figure 4 (p. 15)

key_findings.finding: Speed of onset: conditions in which the drug took effect faster produced more liking or euphoria and also more intoxication and impairment, in healthy social drinkers given diazepam (similar peak blood levels, reached at 61 against 220 minutes; de Wit et al. 1993) and in people with drug-abuse histories given immediate- against extended-release alprazolam (peaks at 1.7 against 9.2 hours; Mumford et al. 1995c). Participants named diazepam's faster onset, compared with oxazepam, as a desirable feature.
key_findings.locator: Rapid speed of onset of drug effect enhances benzodiazepine reinforcing effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: In animals, benzodiazepines were self-injected by a high proportion under suitable conditions (12 of 12 baboons with triazolam) and are intermediate reinforcers: below barbiturates such as pentobarbital, above buspirone and chlorpromazine; of 13 benzodiazepine-receptor ligands tested in baboons with similar methods, only abecarnil did not function as a reinforcer. Oral self-administration was harder to establish (8 of 18 tabulated studies negative).
key_findings.locator: Reinforcing effects of benzodiazepines in laboratory animals: relationship to human data, 2nd paragraph (p. 16, continuing on p. 23) and 4th paragraph (p. 28); Table 6 footnote a (p. 27); Comparison of the self-administration of benzodiazepines to other drugs, 1st paragraph (p. 28); Differences between benzodiazepines, 2nd paragraph (p. 29); Figure 5 (p. 29)
key_findings.note: Eight further oral rat studies that did not clearly show reinforcement are listed only in Table 6 footnote a (p. 27), so 16 of 26 oral studies did not clearly show it (editors' count).

key_findings.finding: Little evidence supports the common belief that physical dependence makes benzodiazepines more reinforcing: in baboons, clear physical dependence did not bring consistent reinforcement, and in monkeys weeks of diazepam pretreatment did not change how hard they worked for diazepam; one human study found that people on long-term therapeutic diazepam switched abruptly to placebo took more unauthorized benzodiazepines, and had more withdrawal symptoms, than people whose dose was tapered (Cappell et al. 1987).
key_findings.locator: The role of physical dependence in benzodiazepine reinforcement, 1st paragraph (p. 29, continuing on p. 30) and 2nd paragraph (p. 30)

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that the risks of long-term use (memory impairment, accidents, falls and hip fractures in older people, withdrawal) are much better documented than its benefits, so that there is little empirical justification for most long-term use, and that what the laboratory preference of moderate drinkers means for real-world risk is unclear.
key_findings.locator: Implications and conclusions, 1st paragraph and 4th paragraph (p. 30, the 4th continuing on p. 31)

reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the count of human studies should be taken from the tables.

reporting_issues.issue: The text twice refers to Figure 7 for baboon intravenous self-injection data, but the paper has five figures and those data are in Figure 5.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor labelling error.

reporting_issues.issue: The text describes five double-blind studies of the reinforcing effects of diazepam in anxious people, but one of the five (Roache et al. 1997) tested alprazolam.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the anxiety evidence covers two benzodiazepines.

reporting_issues.consequence: The negative share of oral studies is understated (16 of 26 by the editors' count).

reporting_issues.issue: Several reinforcer or punisher labels in Table 3 rest on the reviewers' own one-tailed tests against 50% chance (footnotes c and d) rather than on the original analyses, including the label for anxious volunteers in Chutuape & de Wit (1995), described as marginal (P=0.06).
reporting_issues.consequence: The table's labels are more lenient than two-tailed tests in the original articles would be; check primary papers before citing a label.

reporting_issues.issue: For de Wit et al. (1986), Table 3 gives estimated mean choices of 28% for 10 mg diazepam and 73% for amphetamine. De Wit's own printed amphetamine means (4.0, 3.1 and 2.9 of 5 choices) average about 67%, and its Figure 1 bars for 10 mg diazepam read about 1.3, 0.4 and 1.5 of 5, about 22% (editors' reading of de Wit et al., 1986, pp. 536, 540).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite de Wit et al. (1986) for its own figures rather than this table's estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The 7.1% figure for the high-school class of 1995 is cited to a 1995 press release, while the statement that about half of those using tranquilizers usually got high is cited to Johnston et al. (1993), an earlier survey report.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two figures come from different survey years and should not be combined into one estimate.

design_detail: Cross-sectional analysis of the 2015 and 2016 US National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH), the first two years after a questionnaire redesign: 86,186 adults, of whom 10,290 reported past-year benzodiazepine use. Outcomes: past-year use as prescribed and misuse (any use other than as a doctor directed), and, among people reporting misuse, its type, main reason, source and the benzodiazepine misused. Survey-weighted prevalence; multivariable logistic regression for any use (all adults) and for misuse against use as prescribed (people who used benzodiazepines); comparison of people aged 18–49 and 50 or older who reported misuse.
can_establish: National estimates for 2015–2016 of self-reported past-year benzodiazepine use and misuse among US civilian adults living in households, the type, main reasons and sources of misuse that people reported, and the cross-sectional characteristics that went with use and with misuse.
cannot_establish: Why any association exists or in which direction (cross-sectional); whether the reasons people gave are accurate or complete; trends over time (the 2015 redesign prevents comparison with earlier years); use among people in institutions or the military; how much was taken (only days of misuse were analysed); or harms beyond DSM-IV abuse and dependence criteria.

sample.recruitment: NSDUH: an independent multistage area probability sample in all 50 states of the US civilian non-institutionalized population, administered by RTI International and sponsored by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. Two computer-assisted parts: one led by an interviewer and an audio-assisted part answered privately, to encourage honest reporting of illicit drug use (PDF p. 2, Methods, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Respondents aged 18 or older in the 2015 and 2016 survey years, the years available after the 2015 redesign (N=86,186). Benzodiazepine use was identified from answers to the tranquilizer (anxiety or muscle spasm) and sedative (insomnia) items; details are in an online supplement that was not among the files read (PDF p. 2, Methods › Benzodiazepine Use or Misuse, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Weighted: aged 18–25 14.3%, 26–34 15.8%, 35–49 24.9%, 50–64 25.6%, 65 or older 19.4%; women 51.8%; non-Hispanic white 64.6%, non-Hispanic Black 11.8%, Hispanic 15.7%, other 8.0%; Medicaid 14.2%; past-year mental illness mild 9.2%, moderate 4.8%, severe 4.2% (Table 1, PDF p. 4).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (cross-sectional). Response rates for 2015 and 2016 are not reported; the authors mention possible non-response bias and declining NSDUH response rates (Discussion, limitations paragraph, PDF pp. 8–9).
sample.selection_effects: The household frame leaves out institutionalized adults and active-duty military (PDF p. 9), so people in prisons, hospitals, residential treatment and nursing homes are missing. Everything is self-reported without verification, and benzodiazepines count only when named in the tranquilizer and sedative sections. The characteristics of misuse among adults aged 50 or older rest on 176 respondents.

exposure.measurement: Self-report. For each medication class, past-year use as prescribed and past-year misuse, defined since 2015 as use "in any way a doctor did not direct": without a prescription, in greater amounts, more often or longer than prescribed, or in any other way. A respondent with any past-year misuse counts as misusing even if they also used the drug as prescribed. People reporting misuse were asked its type, their reasons (to relax, to experiment, to get high, for sleep, for emotions, to counter the effect of another drug, because they were hooked, or another reason) and the source. Abuse and dependence by DSM-IV criteria (PDF p. 2, Methods › Benzodiazepine Use or Misuse, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Days of misuse in the past month: mean 5.4 (SE 0.3); 5.0 at ages 18–49 and 7.1 at 50 or older (PDF p. 5; Table 3, PDF p. 8). Amounts and routes are not analysed.
exposure.polysubstance: Measured and entered in both models: past-year tobacco; alcohol, marijuana and heroin use or DSM-IV abuse or dependence; prescription opioid and stimulant use as prescribed, misuse, or abuse or dependence (PDF p. 2, Methods › Other Respondent Characteristics; Tables 1–2).

comparison.controls: Any-use model: adults with no past-year benzodiazepine use. Misuse model: people who used benzodiazepines only as prescribed. Characteristics of misuse: ages 18–49 against 50 or older.
comparison.matching: None; multivariable logistic regression with all listed characteristics entered together (major depressive episode and suicidal ideation left out, as NSDUH instructs, because they build the mental illness variable). Interactions with age were tested one characteristic at a time, were significant for three (non-metropolitan area, tobacco, marijuana) and were not entered in the final model (PDF p. 3; Table 2 footnote e, PDF p. 7).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the prevalence estimates. For the correlates: health insurance other than Medicaid, access to care, the condition for which a benzodiazepine was prescribed and prescriber behaviour were not measured, although the discussion attributes some misuse to poor access to care.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The comparison groups include people who use other substances; other use is adjusted for, not excluded.

outcomes.instruments: NSDUH 2015–2016 questionnaire (redesigned in 2015): prescription tranquilizer and sedative sections with the specific medication, type of misuse, reasons and source; DSM-IV abuse and dependence; the NSDUH past-year mental illness variable built from psychological distress, functional impairment, major depressive episode and suicidal ideation items; self-rated health; sociodemographic items (PDF p. 2).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed beyond reference to NSDUH documentation.
outcomes.operationalization: Misuse follows the NSDUH definition, which counts taking one's own prescription more often or longer than directed, and use for symptoms such as sleep or tension. The authors argue that part of what NSDUH counts as misuse may be treatment of untreated symptoms by people with poor access to care (PDF p. 7, Discussion, 4th paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: two-sided tests at alpha .05 (PDF p. 3). 27 counts the two regression outcomes (any use; misuse against use as prescribed) and the 25 younger-against-older comparisons in Table 3 (26 rows; none is tested for theft from a health care setting); about 20 characteristic × age interaction tests were also run.

analysis.effect_sizes: Survey-weighted prevalences with 95% CIs and adjusted odds ratios (Stata 13.1 with NSDUH weights, clustering and strata). Past-year any use 12.6% (12.2–12.9), 30.6 million adults a year (29.7–31.5); use as prescribed 10.4% (10.1–10.7), 25.3 million (24.5–26.1); misuse 2.2% (2.0–2.3), 5.3 million (5.0–5.6); misuse made up 17.2% of use. Misuse by age: 5.2% (4.8–5.6) at 18–25, 3.3% at 26–34, 1.7% at 35–49, 1.4% at 50–64 and 0.6% (0.4–0.8) at 65 or older; among people who used benzodiazepines, the share who misused them was 51.0%, 28.6%, 13.8%, 9.7% and 4.4%. Any use: women 15.4% against men 9.5% (AOR 1.84, 1.72–1.96); severe past-year mental illness 41.5% (AOR 3.80, 3.40–4.26); prescription opioid misuse 35.5% (AOR 4.21, 3.66–4.85) and abuse or dependence 59.9% (AOR 7.34, 5.51–9.76). Misuse rather than use as prescribed: 65 or older against 18–25 AOR 0.23 (0.15–0.34); women 0.74 (0.61–0.90); prescription opioid misuse 4.11 (3.26–5.18) and abuse or dependence 4.81 (3.45–6.72); prescription stimulant misuse 2.46 (1.85–3.27) and abuse or dependence 3.40 (1.72–6.70); alcohol abuse or dependence 2.31 (1.73–3.09); marijuana abuse or dependence 2.39 (1.62–3.52); prescription opioid use as prescribed 0.69 (0.57–0.84); heroin use (0.91, 0.41–2.04) and abuse or dependence (1.20, 0.76–1.91) not significant. Among people reporting misuse (Table 3): without a prescription 73.9%; main reason to relax or relieve tension 47.1%, to help with sleep 26.6%, to get high 11.6%, to help with feelings or emotions 10.1%, to experiment 6.0%; source free from a friend or relative 53.2%, one clinician 19.5%, bought from a friend or relative 12.3%, bought from a dealer or stranger 7.7%; alprazolam 75.1%, diazepam 20.5%, clonazepam 20.0%, lorazepam 15.4%; past-year abuse 4.6% (3.7–5.6) and dependence 6.8% (5.6–8.2).
analysis.covariates: Age group, gender, race-ethnicity, education, household income, Medicaid, metropolitan area, past-year mental illness, self-rated health, tobacco, alcohol, marijuana and heroin categories, and prescription opioid and stimulant categories (Tables 1–2).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Secondary analysis of publicly available, de-identified NSDUH data; no protocol referenced; exempt from IRB review (PDF p. 3).
analysis.selective_reporting: Bivariate results by age are reported only as the three significant interactions; another reason and other sources are not shown in Table 3, whose main-reason percentages add to more than 100%; confidence intervals are printed for only a few age-specific prevalences; how benzodiazepines were identified is described only in an online supplement.
analysis.power: Not discussed. National estimates are precise; characteristics of misuse at 50 or older rest on 176 respondents, with wide intervals for rare categories (for example being hooked, 0.9% against 0.5%, OR 1.89, 0.17–20.72).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 2015–2016, about one in eight US adults living in households (12.6%) reported past-year benzodiazepine use and 2.2% reported misuse; misuse made up 17.2% of use, was most common at ages 18–25 (5.2%, about half of all use at that age) and rare at 65 or older (0.6%). People reporting misuse most often took a benzodiazepine without a prescription (73.9%), most often alprazolam (75.1%), mostly from a friend or relative (about 69% in all), and gave as main reasons relaxing or relieving tension (47.1%) and sleep (26.6%); getting high was named by 11.6% (13.9% at 18–49, 3.0% at 50 or older). Misuse went with misuse and use disorders of other substances, above all prescription opioids and stimulants; 4.6% and 6.8% of people reporting misuse met DSM-IV criteria for abuse and for dependence.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that patients also prescribed stimulants or opioids should be monitored for benzodiazepine misuse (PDF p. 1), but among people who used benzodiazepines, prescribed opioid use went with lower odds of misuse (AOR 0.69, 0.57–0.84) and prescribed stimulant use was not significantly associated with it (AOR 0.90, 0.74–1.09); the strong associations were with misuse and with abuse or dependence of those drugs (Table 2, PDF p. 7; Results, PDF p. 3). The suggestion that misuse partly reflects limited access to care (PDF pp. 7–9) is not tested here: insurance other than Medicaid was not measured, Medicaid and income were not associated with misuse, and the authors note that misuse was not higher in racial and ethnic minority groups with poorer access (PDF p. 8). Use described as higher than previously reported rests on comparisons with surveys of different design, which the authors say may explain the difference (PDF p. 8). That use at 50–64 exceeds use at 65 or older (abstract, conclusions) rests on 14.3% against 12.9% without a test, while the Highlights say it matches.

timeline.event: Earlier review of benzodiazepine reinforcement and long-term use, citing US survey figures from 1990 and 1995.
Becker, Fiellin and Desai: NSDUH 2002–2004 estimate of non-medical use of tranquilizers and sedatives overall, which the authors call similar to their misuse estimate (as cited, PDF p. 8).

Bachhuber and colleagues: 5.6% of US adults filled a benzodiazepine prescription in 2013 (Medical Expenditure Panel Survey), and benzodiazepine-related overdose mortality grew nearly fivefold from 1996 to 2013 (as cited, PDF pp. 1, 8).
Kaufmann and colleagues: benzodiazepine use by 4.2% of adults in NHANES 2013–2014, which asks about the past 30 days (as cited, PDF p. 8).
This study: NSDUH 2015–2016, benzodiazepine-specific use and misuse with reasons and sources.

replication.where_it_stands: Among the papers read, the only national estimate of benzodiazepine-specific misuse with reasons and sources, from the first two years of the redesigned NSDUH. Earlier national figures came from other surveys or pooled tranquilizers and sedatives and are not directly comparable; later NSDUH years would show whether the pattern holds.

Independent multistage area probability sample in all 50 states, analysed with NSDUH weights, clustering and strata.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As a prevalence study it uses a large national probability sample, a consistent instrument and design-based analysis. The constraints that matter are self-report without verification, the frame's exclusions, unreported response rates, and a broad definition of misuse that puts taking a friend's pill to sleep, taking extra of one's own prescription and using to get high in one category. Cite it for 2015–2016 US prevalence of benzodiazepine use and misuse and for the types, reasons and sources people reported; do not cite its correlates as causes or its access-to-care explanation as a finding.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 86,186 adult NSDUH respondents in 2015 and 2016, of whom 10,290 reported past-year benzodiazepine use (7,757 only as prescribed, 2,533 with any misuse; of those with misuse, 2,357 aged 18–49 and 176 aged 50 or older).
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph, and Benzodiazepine Use or Misuse, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 2); Table 1 heading (PDF p. 4); Table 2 heading (PDF p. 6); Table 3 heading (PDF p. 8)

key_findings.finding: An estimated 30.6 million US adults a year (95% CI 29.7–31.5 million), 12.6% (12.2–12.9), used a benzodiazepine in the past year: 10.4% (10.1–10.7) only as prescribed and 2.2% (2.0–2.3) with misuse. Any use was highest at ages 50–64 (14.3%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Prevalence and Predictors of Any Benzodiazepine Use, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 (PDF p. 3); Table 1, Age rows (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Among people who used benzodiazepines, 25.3 million (24.5–26.1) used them as prescribed and 5.3 million (5.0–5.6) reported misuse; misuse made up 17.2% of all use.
key_findings.locator: Results › Prevalence and Predictors of Benzodiazepine Misuse, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3); Table 2, Overall row (PDF p. 6)

key_findings.finding: By age (all adults), use as prescribed was 5.0%, 8.3%, 10.7%, 12.9% and 12.3%, and misuse 5.2% (4.8–5.6), 3.3%, 1.7%, 1.4% and 0.6% (0.4–0.8), at 18–25, 26–34, 35–49, 50–64 and 65 or older. Among people who used benzodiazepines, the share who misused them was 51.0%, 28.6%, 13.8%, 9.7% and 4.4%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Prevalence and Predictors of Benzodiazepine Misuse, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3); Table 2, Age rows (PDF p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Any past-year use was more common in women (15.4% against 9.5%; AOR 1.84, 1.72–1.96) and in non-Hispanic white adults (15.4%; Black 7.2%, AOR 0.45; Hispanic 7.7%, AOR 0.59), and rose with past-year mental illness (none 9.1%; mild 21.5%, AOR 1.93; moderate 29.3%, AOR 2.47; severe 41.5%, AOR 3.80) and with prescription opioid involvement (none 6.8%; prescribed use 20.0%, AOR 2.54; misuse 35.5%, AOR 4.21; abuse or dependence 59.9%, AOR 7.34).
key_findings.locator: Results › Prevalence and Predictors of Any Benzodiazepine Use, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (PDF p. 3); Table 1 (PDF pp. 4–5)

key_findings.finding: Among people who used benzodiazepines, misuse rather than use as prescribed went with younger age (65 or older against 18–25, AOR 0.23, 0.15–0.34), male gender (women 0.74, 0.61–0.90), any tobacco (1.41), alcohol (any 1.42; abuse or dependence 2.31), marijuana (any 1.88; abuse or dependence 2.39), prescription opioid misuse (4.11) and abuse or dependence (4.81), and prescription stimulant misuse (2.46) and abuse or dependence (3.40). Prescribed opioid use went with lower odds (0.69, 0.57–0.84) and fair or poor health with lower odds (0.61); prescribed stimulant use (0.90), heroin, mental illness, income, education and Medicaid were not associated.
key_findings.locator: Results › Prevalence and Predictors of Benzodiazepine Misuse, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 3); Table 2 (PDF pp. 6–7)

key_findings.finding: Type of misuse: without a prescription 73.9% (78.4% at 18–49 against 56.4% at 50 or older; OR 0.36, 0.25–0.51); in greater amounts than prescribed 16.0%; more often than prescribed 10.1% (8.1% against 17.9%; OR 2.47, 1.57–3.90); longer than prescribed 4.9%; in other ways 18.7%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of Misuse Among Younger and Older Adults, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3); Table 3, Type of misuse (PDF p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Main reason for misuse: to relax or relieve tension 47.1%, to help with sleep 26.6%, to get high 11.6%, to help with feelings or emotions 10.1%, to experiment 6.0%, to increase or decrease the effect of another drug 1.6%, hooked or have to have it 0.6%. People aged 50 or older more often named sleep (41.7% against 22.4%; OR 2.48, 1.83–3.35) and less often getting high (3.0% against 13.9%; OR 0.19, p=.003).
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of Misuse Among Younger and Older Adults, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 3); Table 3, Main reason for misuse (PDF p. 8)
key_findings.note: The main-reason percentages add to 103.6% overall (104.0% and 101.3% by age group), and another reason is not shown; whether people could give more than one main reason is not stated.

key_findings.finding: Source of the misused benzodiazepine: free from a friend or relative 53.2%, one clinician 19.5% (14.3% at 18–49 against 38.4% at 50 or older; OR 3.73, 2.65–5.26), bought from a friend or relative 12.3%, bought from a dealer or stranger 7.7%, stolen from a friend or relative 3.3%, two or more clinicians 0.9%, stolen from a health care setting 0.1%. In all, a friend or relative was the source for nearly 70%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of Misuse Among Younger and Older Adults, 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 3, ending on PDF p. 5); Table 3, Source of medication for misuse (PDF p. 8)
key_findings.note: Editors' sum of the three friend-or-relative categories: 68.8%. The sources listed add to 97.0%.

key_findings.finding: Benzodiazepine misused: alprazolam 75.1% (80.3% at 18–49 against 56.4% at 50 or older; OR 0.32), diazepam 20.5% (17.8% against 30.5%; OR 2.04), clonazepam 20.0%, lorazepam 15.4% (12.6% against 26.0%; OR 2.44).
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of Misuse Among Younger and Older Adults, 4th paragraph (PDF p. 5); Table 3, Medication misused (PDF p. 8)

key_findings.finding: People reporting misuse did so on a mean of 5.4 days (SE 0.3) in the past month (5.0 at 18–49, 7.1 at 50 or older); 4.6% (3.7–5.6) met DSM-IV criteria for past-year abuse and 6.8% (5.6–8.2) for past-year dependence.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of Misuse Among Younger and Older Adults, 4th paragraph (PDF p. 5); Table 3, Other characteristics of benzodiazepine misuse (PDF p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Misuse was common among adults with other substance problems: benzodiazepine misuse was reported by 39.6% of adults with prescription stimulant abuse or dependence, 35.6% with prescription opioid abuse or dependence, 40.8% with heroin abuse or dependence, 18.6% with marijuana abuse or dependence and 10.3% with alcohol abuse or dependence, against 0.8% to 2.0% of adults without any use of each of those substances.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, continued, All respondents, Misuse column

key_findings.finding: The authors suggest that a substantial part of what NSDUH counts as misuse may be use for untreated symptoms (insomnia, anxiety) by people with poor access to care, especially younger uninsured adults, and call the link between alcohol abuse or dependence and benzodiazepine misuse particularly concerning because of the higher potential for fatal poisoning when the two are combined.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (PDF p. 7) and 6th paragraph (PDF p. 7, continuing on PDF p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: cross-sectional design; no trends because of the 2015 redesign; possible non-response bias, with declining NSDUH response rates; institutionalized adults and active-duty military not covered.

reporting_issues.issue: The main-reason percentages in Table 3 add to 103.6% overall (104.0% at 18–49 and 101.3% at 50 or older), although each person's main reason is described, and another reason is not shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reasons cannot be read as one main reason per person; claims should give the percentages as printed and say that they add to more than 100%.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 footnote e describes the model's outcome as no benzodiazepine use against any use (as in Table 1), whereas the Table 2 model compares misuse with use as prescribed among people who used benzodiazepines (Methods, PDF p. 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: A labelling error; the odds ratios are those of misuse against use as prescribed, as the Methods and Results state.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 3 the OR column for mean days of misuse in the past month gives 2.10 (−0.30 to 4.51), which is the difference between the means (7.1 − 5.0), not an odds ratio; the interval for getting high is printed as .07 to 56, with a decimal point missing.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the days difference is not significant (p=.09), and the getting-high odds ratio (0.19) reproduces from the printed percentages (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1's vertical axis has ticks every 2 percentage points but labels the tick between 12 and 16 as 15, so the any-use bar for ages 50–64 (14.3% in Table 1) appears to reach 15%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Read values from Tables 1 and 2, not from the figure.

reporting_issues.issue: Response rates for the 2015 and 2016 survey years are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Non-response bias cannot be judged from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and conclusions say use at ages 50–64 now exceeds use at 65 or older, while the Highlights say it matches; the difference (14.3% against 12.9% for any use; 12.9% against 12.3% as prescribed) is not tested.
reporting_issues.consequence: Describe the two age groups as having similar rates unless a test is found.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's conclusion that patients also prescribed stimulants or opioids should be monitored for benzodiazepine misuse does not match Table 2, where, among people who used benzodiazepines, prescribed opioid use went with lower odds of misuse (AOR 0.69, 0.57–0.84) and prescribed stimulant use was not significantly associated with it (AOR 0.90, 0.74–1.09); the associations were with misuse and abuse or dependence of those drugs. (Prescribed opioid and stimulant use did go with higher odds of any benzodiazepine use: AOR 2.54 and 2.11, Table 1.)
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the associations with opioid and stimulant misuse and use disorders, not with prescribed use.
